The player's Mute command loses its default key, and later gets it
back. `set` with `[]` saves an override that unbinds the command
(remembered across launches); `reset` removes the override, so the
command's own default bindings apply again.
```ts
await plugin.bindings.set({ plugin: "host", command: "mute" }, []);
// later
await plugin.bindings.reset({ plugin: "host", command: "mute" });
```

### Clipboard

The system clipboard (`clipboard`). Unavailable without a user interface.

Platforms: macOS writes text as UTF-8 and images as their original
PNG/JPEG bytes; Windows writes Unicode text and images as a bitmap plus
PNG. Other systems: `unsupported`. Failures: `invalid`, `missing`,
`unavailable`, `failed` (the system refused).

The player reads and writes the system clipboard on the plugin's behalf.
Text is plain text; images are written from a PNG or JPEG file.

- @capability clipboard

```ts
interface Clipboard {
  /**
   * Plain text on the clipboard; `null` when it holds none.
   * @capability clipboard
   * @throws unavailable (rejects) The player runs without a user interface.
   * @throws unsupported (rejects) A system other than macOS and Windows.
   * @throws failed (rejects) The system refused (Windows).
   * @throws capability (rejects) The manifest does not declare `clipboard`.
   * @example Open a URL the user copied
   * A "Paste and play" command opens the address on the clipboard. `readText`
   * resolves with the clipboard's text, or `null` when it holds none (an
   * image, nothing).
   * ```ts
   * const text = await plugin.clipboard.readText();
   * if (text?.startsWith("https://")) await plugin.player.open(text.trim());
   * ```
   */
  readText(): Promise<string | null>;
  /**
   * Replace the clipboard with text (at most 1 MiB of UTF-8).
   * @capability clipboard
   * @throws invalid (rejects) More than 1 MiB of UTF-8.
   * @throws unavailable (rejects) The player runs without a user interface.
   * @throws unsupported (rejects) A system other than macOS and Windows.
   * @throws failed (rejects) The system refused.
   * @throws capability (rejects) The manifest does not declare `clipboard`.
   * @example Copy the playing file's path
   * The path of the playing file is put on the clipboard, replacing what was
   * there. It resolves once the system has it.
   * ```ts
   * const { source } = plugin.player.state;
   * if (source) await plugin.clipboard.writeText(source);
   * ```
   */
  writeText(text: string): Promise<void>;
  /**
   * Replace the clipboard with a PNG or JPEG file (absolute path, at most 16 MB).
   * @capability clipboard
   * @throws missing (rejects) The file does not exist.
   * @throws invalid (rejects) Not an absolute path, not PNG or JPEG, over 16 MB, or (Windows) an image the system cannot decode.
   * @throws unavailable (rejects) The player runs without a user interface.
   * @throws unsupported (rejects) A system other than macOS and Windows.
   * @throws failed (rejects) The system refused.
   * @throws capability (rejects) The manifest does not declare `clipboard`.
   * @example Copy a snapshot to the clipboard
   * A frame the plugin saved as PNG is put on the clipboard, ready to paste
   * into another application. The player reads the file and writes the
   * image (macOS: its original bytes; Windows: a bitmap plus PNG).
   * ```ts
   * await plugin.clipboard.writeImage(pngPath); // absolute path, at most 16 MB
   * await plugin.osd.show("Snapshot copied");
   * ```
   */
  writeImage(path: string): Promise<void>;
}
```

Example: Copy the current file and position

The clipboard holds "path @ seconds" for pasting into a note. The
player writes the system clipboard; it rejects with `unsupported` on
systems other than macOS and Windows and `failed` when the system
refuses, which the plugin reports.
```ts
const { source, position } = plugin.player.state;
try {
  await plugin.clipboard.writeText(`${source} @ ${position}`); // data, not shown
} catch (error) {
  void plugin.osd.show("Could not copy: {}", [(error as PluginError).code]);
}
```

### Power

Keeping the computer awake (`playback.control`).

A request, not a command: the player keeps the system awake while any
plugin asks for it and a source plays, and withdraws a plugin's request
when it stops.

- @capability playback.control

```ts
interface Power {
  /**
   * `"playing"`: while a source is ready and not paused, keep the display
   * (video) or the system (audio only) from sleeping. Any plugin asking is
   * enough; a stopped plugin's request is withdrawn.
   *
   * It only registers the request (`invalid` for a bad mode); failures to
   * take the system assertion are logged by the player, not reported.
   * macOS uses `caffeinate`, Windows the thread execution state; elsewhere
   * it has no effect.
   * @capability playback.control
   * @throws invalid (rejects) A mode other than `"off"` or `"playing"`.
   * @throws capability (rejects) The manifest does not declare `playback.control`.
   * @example Follow the plugin's own "Keep awake" setting
   * The plugin keeps the display awake during playback only while its
   * setting is on. Each call replaces this plugin's request; `"off"`
   * withdraws it, and other plugins' requests still count.
   * ```ts
   * const store = plugin.storage.json("power", { defaults: { keepAwake: true } });
   * await plugin.power.preventSleep(store.value.keepAwake ? "playing" : "off");
   * ```
   */
  preventSleep(mode: "off" | "playing"): Promise<void>;
}
```

Example: Keep the display on while playing

The screen does not dim or sleep while a video plays, and may again when
it is paused or ends. The player takes the system's assertion only while
a source is ready and not paused.
```ts
await plugin.power.preventSleep("playing"); // "off" withdraws the request
```

### ToolResult

The output of Tools.run.

```ts
interface ToolResult {
  /** Standard output (at most `maxOutput` bytes). */
  stdout: Uint8Array;
  /** The last 64 KiB of standard error. */
  stderr: string;
}
```

### Tools

`plugin.tools`: ffmpeg and ffprobe, run in this plugin's process. No
capability.

ffmpeg and ffprobe run as child processes of the plugin. When
`VESTRA_FFMPEG` / `VESTRA_FFPROBE` is set, only that path is used (an
invalid one means the tool is not found); otherwise the tool is searched
on `PATH`. A found path is kept for the plugin's run, a miss is looked up
again next time. Disposing the
scope ends a running process.

- @capability None.

```ts
interface Tools {
  /**
   * Run ffmpeg or ffprobe (`VESTRA_FFMPEG` / `VESTRA_FFPROBE` when set, else
   * found on `PATH`) without a shell. Rejects `unavailable` (not found), `timeout`,
   * `failed` (non-zero exit; `message` is the last stderr line), `invalid`
   * (output over `maxOutput`, default 16 MiB), `aborted` (`signal`). Timeout,
   * `signal` and disposing the scope end the process.
   *
   * Arguments are passed as-is (no quoting needed). On Windows `PATHEXT` is
   * honoured. Ending sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 300 ms (immediate on
   * Windows).
   * @capability None.
   * @throws unavailable (rejects) The tool was not found.
   * @throws timeout (rejects) It ran longer than `timeoutMs`; the process is ended.
   * @throws failed (rejects) A non-zero exit; `message` is the last stderr line.
   * @throws invalid (rejects) Bad arguments or options, or output over `maxOutput`.
   * @throws aborted (rejects) `signal` aborted, or the scope was disposed.
   * @example Cut a clip without re-encoding
   * The plugin writes the first ten seconds of the file to a new file. `run`
   * starts ffmpeg without a shell (arguments pass as they are, no quoting)
   * and resolves with its output once it exits with 0; a failure rejects
   * with the last line ffmpeg printed.
   * ```ts
   * await plugin.tools.run(
   *   "ffmpeg",
   *   ["-y", "-i", input, "-t", "10", "-c", "copy", output],
   *   { timeoutMs: 60_000 }, // give up after a minute
   * );
   * ```
   */
  run(tool: "ffmpeg" | "ffprobe", args: string[], options: {
    timeoutMs: number;
    maxOutput?: number;
    signal?: AbortSignal;
  }): Promise<ToolResult>;
  /**
   * Whether the tool can be found.
   * @capability None.
   * @throws Never; it resolves `false` when the tool cannot be found.
   * @example Grey out a command when ffmpeg is missing
   * The Export item is disabled with a reason when ffmpeg is not installed.
   * `available` looks the tool up (a found path is kept, a miss is looked
   * up again on the next call, so installing it later is noticed).
   * ```ts
   * const hasFfmpeg = await plugin.tools.available("ffmpeg");
   * plugin.commands.add({
   *   id: "export",
   *   path: ["@video", "Export…"],
   *   enabled: hasFfmpeg,
   *   // Shown with the greyed-out item.
   *   reason: hasFfmpeg ? null : "Install ffmpeg to export",
   *   run() {},
   * });
   * ```
   */
  available(tool: "ffmpeg" | "ffprobe"): Promise<boolean>;
}
```

Example: Read a file's format with ffprobe

The plugin gets a media file's container details as JSON. `available`
says whether ffprobe can be found (`VESTRA_FFPROBE`, then `PATH`); `run`
starts it from the plugin's own process without a shell and resolves
with its output as bytes once it exits, or rejects when it fails
(`failed`, with the last stderr line) or takes longer than `timeoutMs`.
```ts
if (await plugin.tools.available("ffprobe")) {
  const { stdout } = await plugin.tools.run(
    "ffprobe",
    ["-v", "error", "-show_format", "-of", "json", path],
    { timeoutMs: 10_000 }, // give up on a stuck file after 10 s
  );
  const info = JSON.parse(new TextDecoder().decode(stdout));
  void info.format; // container, duration, bit rate…
}
```

### JsonStore

A JSON file `dataDirectory/<name>.json`, loaded once and saved debounced.

One JSON file, `<dataDirectory>/<name>.json`, made by
Storage.json. `value` is read once when the store is made;
`save` replaces it in memory at once and writes the file `debounceMs`
later (300 by default) through a temporary file and a rename, so a
crash never leaves half a file. Writes to one file run one at a time,
newest last. Disposing the store, its scope or stopping the plugin
writes a pending save first.

- @capability None.

```ts
interface JsonStore<T> extends Disposable {
  /** The loaded value, or `defaults` when the file was missing or broken. */
  readonly value: T;
  /**
   * Replace the value now and write it after `debounceMs`. Only `save` writes: mutating `value` in place is not saved.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Save a slider value without writing on every move
   * Dragging the plugin's volume slider updates the stored value at once but
   * writes the file only once the user stops for 300 ms. Each `save`
   * replaces the value and restarts the debounce timer.
   * ```ts
   * const store = plugin.storage.json("prefs", { defaults: { volume: 100 } });
   * window.on("volumeChanged", (volume: number) => store.save({ ...store.value, volume }));
   * ```
   */
  save(next: T): void;
  /**
   * Write a pending save now.
   * @capability None.
   * @throws Error (rejects) Node's file system error when the file cannot be written; its `code` is Node's (`ENOSPC`, `EACCES` and so on), not a player error code.
   * @example Write the file now before copying it
   * Before exporting its settings, the plugin makes sure the file on disk has
   * the latest value. `flush` writes a pending save at once (or waits for
   * the write in progress) and resolves when the file is written.
   * ```ts
   * const store = plugin.storage.json("settings", { defaults: { step: 5 } });
   * await store.flush(); // the file now has the newest value
   * await copyFile(join(plugin.dataDirectory, "settings.json"), exportPath);
   * ```
   */
  flush(): Promise<void>;
}
```

Example: Count how often the plugin was started

The counter grows by one at every start and is kept in `stats.json`. The
store reads the file when it is made (the defaults when there is none),
and `save` writes the new count a moment later.
```ts
const stats = plugin.storage.json("stats", { defaults: { starts: 0 } });
stats.save({ starts: stats.value.starts + 1 }); // written 300 ms later
```

### Storage

`plugin.storage`: JSON settings files. No capability.

Two kinds of storage, both private to the plugin and needing no
capability. Storage.json keeps settings in JSON files in the
plugin's data directory: they last across player restarts and upgrades,
and are written by the plugin's own process. Storage.session
keeps values in the player's memory for one player run: they survive a
restart of the plugin's process but not of the player. Secrets belong in
Secrets, never in either.

- @capability None.

```ts
interface Storage {
  /**
   * Open `<name>.json` (`name`: 1–64 of `a-z 0-9 -`). A file that cannot be
   * parsed or fails `validate` is renamed `<name>.json.bad-<timestamp>` and
   * `defaults` is used. Writes go to a temporary file, then a rename. Disposal
   * (and stopping the plugin) flushes first.
   *
   * The file is read synchronously on creation; `debounceMs` defaults to
   * 300. Files are created with mode 0600. `invalid` for a bad name.
   * @capability None.
   * @throws invalid (throws) A bad `name`, or a `debounceMs` that is not a non-negative number.
   * @example Keep settings and a recent list in a JSON file
   * The plugin remembers whether to resume and the last ten files across
   * restarts. `json` reads `settings.json` from the data directory at once
   * (or uses `defaults` when it is missing or fails `validate`); `save`
   * replaces the value and writes the file 300 ms later, and stopping the
   * plugin writes a pending save first.
   * ```ts
   * type Settings = { resume: boolean; recent: string[] };
   * const store = plugin.storage.json<Settings>("settings", {
   *   defaults: { resume: true, recent: [] },
   *   validate: (v): v is Settings =>
   *     typeof v === "object" && v !== null && typeof (v as Settings).resume === "boolean",
   * });
   * // Only `save` writes: changing `store.value` in place is not saved.
   * store.save({ ...store.value, recent: [path, ...store.value.recent].slice(0, 10) });
   * ```
   */
  json<T>(name: string, options: {
    defaults: T;
    validate?: (value: unknown) => value is T;
    debounceMs?: number;
  }): JsonStore<T>;
  /**
   * Values the player keeps in its memory for this plugin until the player quits: they survive a restart of the plugin's process (reload, upgrade, crash, failed start) but not the player. See SessionStorage.
   */
  readonly session: SessionStorage;
}
```

Example: Keep a setting across restarts and a queue for this run

The plugin's step size survives a restart of the player; its work queue
survives a reload of the plugin but starts empty with the next player
run. The JSON store reads its file at once and writes it shortly after
each `save`; session values live in the player process.
```ts
const settings = plugin.storage.json("settings", { defaults: { step: 5 } });
const queue = (await plugin.storage.session.get<string[]>("queue")) ?? [];
void settings.value.step; // read synchronously, from the file or the defaults
void queue;
```

### SessionStorage

`plugin.storage.session`: JSON values that live as long as the **player**,
not as long as the plugin's process (like `chrome.storage.session`). No
capability; needs player 0.5.5 (older players reject the calls with
`unsupported`).

`activate` can run more than once in one player session: the player stops
and starts a plugin's process again when the plugin is reloaded (also a
development load with `--plugin`) or upgraded, and after a crash or a
failed start. A later player may also restart plugins that share a
process, or stop an idle plugin and start it on its next use. Variables do
not survive that; keep state that must survive a restart here (or in
storage.json when it must also survive the player
quitting).

| | Values |
| --- | --- |
| The plugin's process restarts: reload, upgrade, crash | kept |
| The plugin failed to start or failed, and starts again | kept |
| The user disables the plugin, or uninstalls it | cleared |
| The player quits | cleared |

- **Per plugin.** A plugin sees only its own keys. Like
  dataDirectory, the values belong to the
  installation: a development load (`--plugin`) has its own.
- **JSON.** `set` stores what `JSON.stringify(value)` writes, and `get`
  returns that, parsed: `undefined` object properties are dropped, a `Date`
  comes back as a string, `NaN` as `null`. **The order of an object's
  properties is not kept**: they may come back in another order. A value
  `JSON.stringify` cannot write (`undefined`, a function, a cycle, a
  `BigInt`) or a string with a lone surrogate (`"\uD800"`) fails with
  `invalid`. The value is not checked when it comes back: after an upgrade
  an older version's value may be read, so check its shape when it matters.
- **Bounded.** Keys are 1–1024 bytes of text. A plugin holds at most 1 MiB,
  counting every key, its value as compact JSON and 128 bytes per key
  (SESSION_STORAGE_LIMITS); a
  `set` beyond it fails with `limit` and changes nothing. One `set` is
  also one message to the player, at most 1 MiB with its key, so a single
  value is a little smaller than that; a larger one fails with `limit`.
  Split large state over several keys.
- **Each call is one request.** A `set` is kept once its promise
  resolves, so a crash right after loses nothing; there is no debounce.
  Calls answer in order.

The player keeps the values in its own memory, per plugin, until it
quits; the plugin's process may restart in between. Each call is one
request to the player, answered in order, with no debounce.

- @capability None.

```ts
interface SessionStorage {
  /**
   * The value stored under `key`, or `undefined` when there is none.
   * @capability None.
   * @throws invalid (rejects) A bad key (empty, over 1024 bytes, with NUL or a lone surrogate).
   * @throws disabled (rejects) The plugin is stopping.
   * @throws unsupported (rejects) A player before 0.5.5.
   * @example Pick up where the plugin stopped after a reload
   * After a reload the plugin resumes the item it was working on. `get`
   * asks the player and resolves with the value parsed from JSON, or
   * `undefined` when nothing is stored; the value is not checked, so its
   * shape is checked here.
   * ```ts
   * const current = await plugin.storage.session.get<{ url: string }>("current");
   * if (typeof current?.url === "string") await plugin.osd.show("Resuming {}", [current.url]);
   * ```
   */
  get<T = unknown>(key: string): Promise<T | undefined>;
  /**
   * Store or replace `value` under `key`. `invalid` for a bad key or a value that is not JSON, `limit` when the plugin's values would be over 1 MiB or the request over the 1 MiB message limit.
   * @capability None.
   * @throws invalid (rejects) A bad key, or a value JSON cannot hold (or a string with a lone surrogate).
   * @throws disabled (rejects) The plugin is stopping.
   * @throws unsupported (rejects) A player before 0.5.5.
   * @throws limit (rejects) The plugin's values would pass 1 MiB, or the request the 1 MiB message limit; nothing changes.
   * @example Remember the item being worked on
   * The plugin records the URL it is processing, so a reload can continue
   * with it. The value is stored as `JSON.stringify` writes it, and is kept
   * once the promise resolves.
   * ```ts
   * await plugin.storage.session.set("current", { url: "https://example.com/a.mkv" });
   * ```
   */
  set(key: string, value: unknown): Promise<void>;
  /**
   * Remove a key; removing a missing one is fine.
   * @capability None.
   * @throws invalid (rejects) A bad key.
   * @throws disabled (rejects) The plugin is stopping.
   * @throws unsupported (rejects) A player before 0.5.5.
   * @example Forget the item once it is done
   * When the work finishes, the plugin removes the entry so that a later
   * reload does not resume it. Removing a key that is not there is fine.
   * ```ts
   * await plugin.storage.session.delete("current");
   * ```
   */
  delete(key: string): Promise<void>;
  /**
   * The keys stored, in code point order.
   * @capability None.
   * @throws disabled (rejects) The plugin is stopping.
   * @throws unsupported (rejects) A player before 0.5.5.
   * @example Clear everything the plugin stored for this run
   * The plugin starts its session state over. `keys` lists the plugin's own
   * keys in code point order; each `delete` is a request of its own.
   * ```ts
   * const session = plugin.storage.session;
   * for (const key of await session.keys()) await session.delete(key);
   * ```
   */
  keys(): Promise<string[]>;
}
```

Example: Keep a work queue across a plugin restart

A download queue survives the plugin being reloaded or crashing, and is
empty again when the player starts next time. Session storage lives in
the player process for one player run; each `set` is kept once its
promise resolves, so nothing is lost if the plugin dies right after.
```ts
// A queue the plugin is working through: after a reload or a crash it
// goes on where it stopped, after the player quits it starts afresh.
const pending = (await plugin.storage.session.get<string[]>("queue")) ?? [];
pending.push("https://example.com/a.mkv");
await plugin.storage.session.set("queue", pending);
```

### System

`plugin.system`: files and links, executed by the player. No capability.
Other systems than macOS and Windows: `unsupported`.

The player opens files, folders and links with the system's own
applications for the plugin, so the plugin never runs `open`,
`explorer` or a shell itself.

- @capability None.

```ts
interface System {
  /**
   * Select files or folders in the file manager (macOS: one Finder window for all, so several files of one folder are all highlighted; Windows: one Explorer window per folder, selecting its first path). Paths that do not exist are skipped; `missing` when none exists; at most 256.
   * @capability None.
   * @throws missing (rejects) None of the paths exists.
   * @throws invalid (rejects) No paths, or more than 256.
   * @throws failed (rejects) The system refused.
   * @throws timeout (rejects) macOS did not answer within 10 s.
   * @throws unsupported (rejects) A system other than macOS and Windows.
   * @example Show the exported files in the file manager
   * After an export, the file manager opens with the new files selected.
   * Paths that no longer exist are skipped; the call rejects with `missing`
   * only when none of them exists.
   * ```ts
   * await plugin.system.reveal(exported); // macOS: one Finder window for all
   * ```
   */
  reveal(paths: string | string[]): Promise<void>;
  /**
   * Open the file or folder with its default application. `missing` if absent.
   * @capability None.
   * @throws missing (rejects) The path does not exist.
   * @throws invalid (rejects) An empty path.
   * @throws failed (rejects) The system refused.
   * @throws timeout (rejects) macOS did not answer within 10 s.
   * @throws unsupported (rejects) A system other than macOS and Windows.
   * @example Open the plugin's data folder
   * A "Show data folder" command opens the plugin's data directory in the
   * file manager, which is the default application for a folder.
   * ```ts
   * await plugin.system.openPath(plugin.dataDirectory);
   * ```
   */
  openPath(path: string): Promise<void>;
  /**
   * Open an http(s) address in the default browser. `invalid` for another protocol or a malformed address; `timeout` after 10 s, `failed` otherwise.
   * @capability None.
   * @throws invalid (rejects) Not an `http:` or `https:` address.
   * @throws timeout (rejects) macOS did not hand it to the browser within 10 s.
   * @throws failed (rejects) The system refused.
   * @throws unsupported (rejects) A system other than macOS and Windows.
   * @example Open the plugin's help page
   * A Help command opens the plugin's documentation in the default browser.
   * Only `http:` and `https:` addresses are opened.
   * ```ts
   * await plugin.system.openUrl("https://example.com/plugin/help");
   * ```
   */
  openUrl(url: string): Promise<void>;
}
```

Example: Show an exported file and open the help page

The file manager opens with the exported file selected, then the
browser opens the plugin's help page. The player performs both on the
plugin's behalf; they reject with `unsupported` on systems other than
macOS and Windows, which the plugin turns into a message.
```ts
try {
  await plugin.system.reveal(exportedFile);
  await plugin.system.openUrl("https://example.com/help");
} catch (error) {
  if ((error as PluginError).code !== "unsupported") throw error;
  await plugin.osd.show(`Saved to ${exportedFile}`); // no file manager to open
}
```

### Secrets

Per-plugin secrets (API keys, passwords) in the system's secret store:
the login keychain on macOS, the Credential Manager on Windows. Needs
`secrets`. `unsupported` on systems without a store, `unavailable` when
the store cannot be reached (no keychain, a read-only store, no logged-in
session on Windows): keep a fallback (or ask again).

The user denying access and other system errors reject `failed`. Never
write secrets to settings files.

Values are stored by the player in the system's secret store under this
plugin's id: other plugins cannot read them. Names are 1–64 of
`a-z 0-9 . _ -`, values 1–1024 bytes of text, at most 256 names per
plugin (`SECRET_LIMITS`).

- @capability secrets

```ts
interface Secrets {
  /**
   * The stored value, `null` when there is none.
   * @capability secrets
   * @throws unsupported (rejects) The system has no secret store.
   * @throws unavailable (rejects) The store cannot be reached (no keychain, a read-only store, no logged-in session on Windows).
   * @throws failed (rejects) The user denied access, or another system error.
   * @throws capability (rejects) The manifest does not declare `secrets`.
   * @throws invalid (rejects) A bad name.
   * @example Read a stored token
   * The plugin uses the token the user saved earlier, or asks for one when
   * there is none. `get` resolves with the stored text or `null`.
   * ```ts
   * const token = await plugin.secrets.get("api-token");
   * if (token === null) await plugin.osd.show("Sign in first");
   * ```
   */
  get(name: string): Promise<string | null>;
  /**
   * Store or replace (`name`: 1–64 of `a-z 0-9 . _ -`; value 1–1024 bytes). At most 256 different names per plugin: a new name beyond that rejects `limit`. Uninstalling with `removeData` deletes them.
   * @capability secrets
   * @throws invalid (rejects) A bad name, or a value that is empty, has NUL or is over 1024 bytes.
   * @throws limit (rejects) A new name beyond 256.
   * @throws unsupported (rejects) The system has no secret store.
   * @throws unavailable (rejects) The store cannot be reached (no keychain, a read-only store, no logged-in session on Windows).
   * @throws failed (rejects) The user denied access, or another system error.
   * @throws capability (rejects) The manifest does not declare `secrets`.
   * @example Save the token the user entered
   * The token the user typed is kept in the system's secret store for later
   * runs. `set` stores or replaces it; the store can refuse, in which case
   * the plugin keeps the token for this run only.
   * ```ts
   * await plugin.secrets.set("api-token", token).catch((error: PluginError) => {
   *   // No store, or access denied: the token is not kept for next time.
   *   void plugin.osd.show("The token could not be saved ({})", [error.code]);
   * });
   * ```
   */
  set(name: string, value: string): Promise<void>;
  /**
   * Remove; removing a missing secret is fine.
   * @capability secrets
   * @throws invalid (rejects) A bad name.
   * @throws unsupported (rejects) The system has no secret store.
   * @throws unavailable (rejects) The store cannot be reached (no keychain, a read-only store, no logged-in session on Windows).
   * @throws failed (rejects) The user denied access, or another system error.
   * @throws capability (rejects) The manifest does not declare `secrets`.
   * @example Sign out by removing the token
   * Signing out removes the stored token, so the next start asks again.
   * Removing a name that is not stored is fine.
   * ```ts
   * await plugin.secrets.delete("api-token");
   * ```
   */
  delete(name: string): Promise<void>;
}
```

Example: Ask for an API token once and keep it in the keychain

The user types the token the first time; later runs read it from the
system's secret store. `get` resolves `null` when nothing is stored; a
store that is missing or refuses access rejects (`unsupported`,
`unavailable`, `failed`), and then the plugin keeps the token for this
run only and asks again next time.
```ts
let token: string | null = null;
try {
  token = await plugin.secrets.get("api-token");
} catch {
  // No usable store: fall through and ask.
}
if (token === null) {
  token = await askUser();
  if (token)
    await plugin.secrets.set("api-token", token).catch(() => {}); // best effort
}
```

### RenderingMode

Which renderer draws the video: `"gpu"` (the GPU renderer, where
render options apply) or `"software"` (they fail
with `unsupported`). The same values as SystemInfo.rendering.

- @player 0.5.13

```ts
type RenderingMode = "gpu" | "software";
```

Example: Tell the user which renderer draws the video

The plugin shows "Rendering: GPU" or "Rendering: software" on the
video. `state()` asks the player; `mode` is the renderer drawing now,
which can differ from the saved choice until the next start.
```ts
const { mode } = await plugin.rendering.state();
const label: Record<RenderingMode, string> = { gpu: "GPU", software: "software" };
await plugin.osd.show("Rendering: {}", [label[mode]]);
```

### RenderingPreference

The user's saved rendering choice: `"auto"` (the player decides: the GPU
where this system has a GPU renderer that is not ruled out, software
elsewhere), `"gpu"` or `"software"`. It applies from the next start.

- @player 0.5.13

```ts
type RenderingPreference = "auto" | "gpu" | "software";
```

Example: Describe the saved choice on a settings page

The plugin turns the saved choice into the words its settings page
shows. `preference` is what the user chose, not what draws now:
RenderingState.nextMode says what the next start will use.
```ts
const { preference } = await plugin.rendering.state();
// One word per choice; the Record type makes sure none is missing.
const words: Record<RenderingPreference, string> = {
  auto: "Automatic",
  gpu: "GPU",
  software: "Software",
};
console.log(words[preference]);
```

### RenderingReasonCode

Why the player renders the way it does, as a stable kebab-case code. A
newer player may add codes: compare with the ones you handle and show
RenderingReason.message for the rest. The codes of player 0.5.13:

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `default` | Nothing ruled the GPU out; the platform's default. |
| `pending` | GPU rendering is starting. |
| `headless` | The player runs without a user interface. |
| `no-gpu-backend` | This player has no GPU renderer on this system (Windows today). |
| `env` | The environment chose it (`VESTRA_RENDER`, `VESTRA_SOFTWARE_RENDER`). |
| `preference` | The user chose software rendering (Rendering.setPreference); GPU chosen and available reports `default`. |
| `denylist` | The graphics driver is on the player's denylist. |
| `previous-crash` | GPU rendering crashed at an earlier start; it is tried again after a driver or player update, or after 7 days. |
| `init-failed` | GPU rendering could not start. |
| `window-fallback` | A window could not show GPU frames; the player switched to software during the run. |

- @player 0.5.13

```ts
type RenderingReasonCode = "default" | "pending" | "headless" | "no-gpu-backend" | "env" | "preference" | "denylist" | "previous-crash" | "init-failed" | "window-fallback" | (string & {});
```

Example: Explain a driver problem differently from a user choice

The plugin adds advice only when the graphics driver is the cause.
`reason.code` is looked up among the codes the plugin knows; an unknown
code from a newer player falls through to the player's own message.
```ts
const { reason } = await plugin.rendering.state();
// Advice for the codes this plugin knows; any other code shows the message.
const advice: Partial<Record<RenderingReasonCode, string>> = {
  denylist: "Update the graphics driver to use the GPU.",
  "previous-crash": "The GPU renderer crashed earlier; it is retried after an update.",
};
console.log(advice[reason.code] ?? reason.message);
```

### RenderingReason

Why the player renders, or will render, the way it does: a stable
RenderingReasonCode to branch on and a sentence to show.

- @player 0.5.13

```ts
interface RenderingReason {
  /** The reason as a stable kebab-case code; branch on this. */
  readonly code: RenderingReasonCode;
  /** The reason as English text for people, for example with the graphics adapter's name and driver version; never branch on it. */
  readonly message: string;
}
```

Example: Show why GPU rendering is off

The plugin logs the player's explanation when the video is drawn in
software. `message` is the player's English text and may name the
graphics adapter and driver version; `code` is for decisions.
```ts
const { mode, reason } = await plugin.rendering.state();
if (mode === "software") console.log(`${reason.code}: ${reason.message}`);
```

### RenderingState

What Rendering.state and Rendering.setPreference report:
the renderer drawing now and why, the saved choice, what the next start
will use, and whether `"gpu"` can be chosen.

- @player 0.5.13

```ts
interface RenderingState {
  /** The renderer drawing the video now; the same as SystemInfo.rendering. */
  readonly mode: RenderingMode;
  /** Why RenderingState.mode is what it is now. */
  readonly reason: RenderingReason;
  /** The saved choice; it applies from the next start. */
  readonly preference: RenderingPreference;
  /** The renderer the next start will use, as far as the player knows now: from the saved choice, the environment, the driver denylist and an earlier GPU crash. */
  readonly nextMode: RenderingMode;
  /** Why the next start will use RenderingState.nextMode. */
  readonly nextReason: RenderingReason;
  /**
   * `true` while RenderingState.nextMode differs from the mode this run started with, so a restart would change the renderer; `false` again when the user changes the choice back.
   */
  readonly restartPending: boolean;
  /** Whether the user can choose `"gpu"` now. */
  readonly gpu: {
    /** `true` when `setPreference("gpu")` would be accepted. */
    readonly available: boolean;
    /** Why `"gpu"` cannot be chosen (`no-gpu-backend`, `headless`, `denylist`, `previous-crash`…); `null` while it is available. */
    readonly reason: RenderingReason | null;
  };
}
```

Example: Label a menu item while a change waits for a restart

The plugin adds "(Restart to Apply)" to its GPU item after the user
changed the choice. `restartPending` compares the mode the next start
will use with the mode this run started with, so it turns false again
when the user changes the choice back.
```ts
const state = await plugin.rendering.state();
const title = state.restartPending
  ? "GPU Rendering (Experimental) (Restart to Apply)"
  : "GPU Rendering (Experimental)";
console.log(title, state.nextMode, state.nextReason.message);
```

### Rendering

`plugin.rendering`: the player's rendering choice, GPU or software.
Reading it needs no capability; changing the saved choice and restarting
the player need `rendering.manage`.

The choice works like a browser's hardware acceleration switch: the
player saves it in its own settings at once, and the running player
keeps its renderer. The next start uses it, whether the user restarts
now through Rendering.restartPlayer or quits and starts the
player later. The player can still rule the GPU out at a start (an
environment variable, a graphics driver on its denylist, a GPU crash at
an earlier start); RenderingState.nextMode and
RenderingState.nextReason say what the next start will do.

The renderer is a choice for the whole player and a restart stops every
plugin, so change it only when the user asks. A plugin that only needs
to know whether render options work reads SystemInfo.rendering.

Players before 0.5.13 do not know these requests: `state()` rejects with
`unsupported`, and they do not load a plugin that declares
`rendering.manage` (an unknown capability). Declare
`"minPlayerVersion": "0.5.13"` when the plugin needs this.

- @capability None to read the state; `rendering.manage` to change the choice or restart the player.
- @player 0.5.13; older players reject the requests as unknown (`unsupported`).

```ts
interface Rendering {
  /**
   * Read the renderer drawing now, the saved choice, what the next start will use and whether `"gpu"` can be chosen. No capability.
   * @capability None.
   * @throws unsupported (rejects) A player before 0.5.13, which does not know the request.
   * @example Find out whether the GPU can be chosen
   * The plugin reads the state once while it starts and keeps it for its
   * menu. Each call asks the player; `gpu.available` is false, with a
   * reason, where this player has no GPU renderer, without a user
   * interface, or when the driver is ruled out. An older player rejects
   * with `unsupported`, and the plugin then offers nothing.
   * ```ts
   * const state = await plugin.rendering.state().catch((error: PluginError) => {
   *   if (error.code === "unsupported") return null; // a player before 0.5.13
   *   throw error;
   * });
   * if (state && !state.gpu.available) console.log(state.gpu.reason?.message);
   * ```
   */
  state(): Promise<RenderingState>;
  /**
   * Save the user's rendering choice. The player writes it to its settings at once; the running player keeps its renderer, and the next start uses the choice whether or not the user restarts now. `"auto"` and `"software"` are always accepted.
   * @param preference - `"auto"`, `"gpu"` or `"software"`.
   * @returns The new state; RenderingState.restartPending tells whether a restart would change the renderer.
   * @capability rendering.manage
   * @throws invalid (rejects) `preference` is not `"auto"`, `"gpu"` or `"software"`.
   * @throws unsupported (rejects) `"gpu"` where this player has no GPU renderer on this system, or runs without a user interface; also any value on a player before 0.5.13.
   * @throws unavailable (rejects) `"gpu"` while it is ruled out: the graphics driver is on the player's denylist, or GPU rendering crashed at an earlier start. The message says which, with the adapter's name and the driver version.
   * @throws failed (rejects) The player could not write its settings file.
   * @throws capability (rejects) The manifest does not declare `rendering.manage`.
   * @example Switch back to the automatic choice
   * A Reset item returns the renderer to the player's own choice and tells
   * the user when it takes effect. `setPreference` saves the choice and
   * resolves with the new state; `restartPending` is true when the next
   * start will draw differently from this run. A refused save leaves the
   * old choice in place.
   * ```ts
   * try {
   *   const state = await plugin.rendering.setPreference("auto");
   *   if (state.restartPending) await plugin.osd.show("Applies after a restart");
   * } catch (error) {
   *   // `failed`: the player's settings file could not be written.
   *   await plugin.osd.show("Not saved ({})", [(error as PluginError).code]);
   * }
   * ```
   */
  setPreference(preference: RenderingPreference): Promise<RenderingState>;
  /**
   * Restart the player so that a changed choice applies now. Resolves once the player has accepted; the player then quits normally, which stops every plugin (this one included), and starts again with the same plugins. A local file that was open continues at its position, paused or playing as it was; a stream or another source that is not a file is not reopened.
   * @capability rendering.manage
   * @throws unsupported (rejects) The player runs without a user interface; also a player before 0.5.13.
   * @throws busy (rejects) A restart is already under way, or this player was itself started by a restart less than 30 seconds ago (so a plugin that restarts on activation cannot make a loop).
   * @throws failed (rejects) The new player process could not be started; the player keeps running.
   * @throws capability (rejects) The manifest does not declare `rendering.manage`.
   * @example Restart after asking the user
   * After the user changed the renderer, the plugin offers to restart now.
   * `confirm` asks first, because a restart closes every window (it needs
   * `ui.dialog`); once `restartPlayer` resolves, the player is quitting and
   * will stop this plugin, so nothing else is started after it.
   * ```ts
   * const { confirmed } = await plugin.dialogs.confirm({
   *   message: "Restart the player now?",
   *   detail: "The new renderer is used from the restart on. The video continues where it is.",
   *   confirm: "Restart",
   * });
   * if (confirmed)
   *   await plugin.rendering.restartPlayer().catch((error: PluginError) => {
   *     // `failed`: the new player could not start; this one keeps running.
   *     void plugin.osd.show("Could not restart ({})", [error.code]);
   *   });
   * ```
   */
  restartPlayer(): Promise<void>;
}
```

Example: Offer GPU rendering as a menu item

Settings ▸ GPU Rendering (Experimental) carries a check mark while the
next start will draw on the GPU, is greyed out with the player's reason
where the GPU cannot be chosen, and saves the other choice when picked.
`state()` reads the player's view once; `setPreference` saves the choice
and resolves with the new state, which the item's bound values read
again after the handler. The how-to guide adds the restart.
```ts
let state = await plugin.rendering.state();
plugin.commands.add({
  id: "gpu-rendering",
  path: ["@settings", "GPU Rendering (Experimental)"],
  checked: () => state.nextMode === "gpu", // also for "auto" on a GPU system
  enabled: () => state.gpu.available,
  reason: () => state.gpu.reason?.message ?? null, // shown while disabled
  run: async () => {
    const choice = state.nextMode === "gpu" ? "software" : "gpu";
    state = await plugin.rendering.setPreference(choice);
  },
});
```

### VideoNode

One node of a VideoFilter chain, by `kind`. Values outside the
ranges below fail with `invalid`. Fields marked "live" change in place
while playing; changing any other field rebuilds the stage (the picture
may stall for one frame), so drive sliders with live fields.

Nodes act after the player's own orientation handling (container
rotation): a portrait video is upright before `transform` runs. At most
64 nodes across all plugins.

```ts
type VideoNode = 
/** FFmpeg `eq`; every field is live. */
{
  /** The node type. */
  kind: "eq";
  /** −1–1, 0 = unchanged. */
  brightness: number;
  /** 0–2, 1 = unchanged. */
  contrast: number;
  /** 0–2, 1 = unchanged. */
  saturation: number;
  /** 0.5–2, 1 = unchanged. */
  gamma: number;
}
/** Gaussian blur (FFmpeg `gblur`). */
 | {
  /** The node type. */
  kind: "gblur";
  /** 0–10 (live). */
  sigma: number;
  /** Always 3. */
  steps: 3;
}
/** Hue rotation; changes in place while playing. */
 | {
  /** The node type. */
  kind: "hue";
  /** −180–180 (live). */
  degrees: number;
}
/** unsharp: 3×3 (`small`) or 7×7 (`large`) luma matrix. */
 | {
  /** The node type. */
  kind: "sharpen";
  /** 0–2. */
  amount: number;
  /** Matrix size. */
  size: "small" | "large";
}
/** hqdn3d strengths. */
 | {
  /** The node type. */
  kind: "denoise";
  /** 0–20 (0 = off). */
  lumaSpatial: number;
  /** 0–20 (0 = off). */
  chromaSpatial: number;
  /** 0–20 (0 = off). */
  lumaTemporal: number;
  /** 0–20 (0 = off). */
  chromaTemporal: number;
}
/** FFmpeg `deblock`. */
 | {
  /** The node type. */
  kind: "deblock";
  /** Filter strength. */
  strength: "weak" | "strong";
}
/** FFmpeg `deband`. */
 | {
  /** The node type. */
  kind: "deband";
  /** 0.003–0.5, the same for all four planes. */
  threshold: number;
  /** Integer 1–64. */
  range: number;
}
/** Applied after the player's own source orientation. */
 | {
  /** The node type. */
  kind: "transform";
  /** Clockwise degrees; applied before the flips. */
  rotate: 0 | 90 | 180 | 270;
  /** Mirror horizontally. */
  flipH: boolean;
  /** Mirror vertically. */
  flipV: boolean;
}
/**
 * Deinterlacing. `interlaced` and `all` are FFmpeg BWDIF in the chain;
 * `field` doubles the frame rate.
 *
 * `when: "auto"` (player 0.5.4) is the player's own deinterlacer instead:
 * decided per frame from the decoder's interlaced flag, with the decoder's
 * hardware deinterlacer where frames stay on the GPU; progressive frames
 * pass untouched. It needs no frames in memory, so a chain with only this
 * node keeps zero-copy hardware decoding (any other node still needs a
 * copy back to memory). It always outputs one frame per field, so it
 * takes `output: "field"` only (`"frame"` fails with `invalid`). It runs
 * before every plugin's chain wherever it is written, and is shared: on
 * while any plugin's chain has one. A chain with it has no other
 * `deinterlace` node. Snapshots and exports deinterlace the same frames
 * with BWDIF at field rate. Players before 0.5.4 refuse `auto` with
 * `invalid`.
 */
 | {
  /** The node type. */
  kind: "deinterlace";
  /** `interlaced`: only frames flagged interlaced; `all`: every frame; `auto`: the player's deinterlacer, on frames flagged interlaced. */
  when: "interlaced" | "all" | "auto";
  /** One frame per frame, or one per field (double rate); `when: "auto"` takes `field` only. */
  output: "frame" | "field";
}
/** Crop to / pad to a display aspect; x, y place it (−1 left/top … 1 right/bottom). */
 | {
  /** The node type. */
  kind: "reframe";
  /** Crop the picture, or pad it with black bars. */
  mode: "crop" | "pad";
  /** Target display aspect 0.25–4. */
  aspect: number;
  /** −1 (left) … 0 (centre) … 1 (right). */
  x: number;
  /** −1 (top) … 0 (centre) … 1 (bottom). */
  y: number;
}
/** Blended frame-rate conversion (FFmpeg `framerate`), an integer 24–120. At most one across all plugins; the player runs it after every chain. */
 | {
  /** The node type. */
  kind: "frameBlend";
  /** Output frame rate, integer 24–120. */
  fps: number;
};
```

Example: Brighten, sharpen and rotate the picture

The video plays a little brighter and more saturated, slightly sharper
and turned a quarter clockwise. The nodes run in array order; `set` sends
the whole chain as this plugin's desired value (last write wins), and the
player applies it to every source until it changes, needing
`processing.video`, `playback.read` and `events`.
```ts
const chain: VideoNode[] = [
  // Live fields: moving them later changes the picture in place.
  { kind: "eq", brightness: 0.05, contrast: 1.1, saturation: 1.2, gamma: 1 },
  // Not live: changing `amount` later rebuilds the stage (a one-frame stall).
  { kind: "sharpen", amount: 0.5, size: "small" },
  { kind: "transform", rotate: 90, flipH: false, flipV: false },
];
plugin.video.filter("picture").set(chain);
```

### AudioNode

One node of an AudioFilter chain, by `kind`. Values outside the
ranges fail with `invalid`; "live" fields change in place while playing.

```ts
type AudioNode = 
/** FFmpeg `volume`. */
{
  /** The node type. */
  kind: "volume";
  /** −60–0 dB (live). */
  gainDb: number;
}
/** One peaking equalizer band (FFmpeg `equalizer`). */
 | {
  /** The node type. */
  kind: "equalizer";
  /** Centre frequency 20–20000 Hz. */
  frequency: number;
  /** Always 1. */
  q: 1;
  /** −6–6 dB (live). */
  gainDb: number;
}
/** Treble shelf (FFmpeg `treble`). */
 | {
  /** The node type. */
  kind: "treble";
  /** Always 3000 Hz. */
  frequency: 3000;
  /** Always 0.5. */
  slope: 0.5;
  /** 0–6 dB (live). */
  gainDb: number;
}
/** Dynamic loudness normalization (FFmpeg `dynaudnorm`); every field is live. */
 | {
  /** The node type. */
  kind: "dynaudnorm";
  /** On or off. */
  enabled: boolean;
  /** Maximum gain 1–4. */
  maxGain: number;
  /** Target peak 0.5–0.95. */
  peak: number;
}
/** Routing on a stereo mix (more channels are mixed down first). */
 | {
  /** The node type. */
  kind: "channels";
  /** `stereo` leaves it unchanged. */
  mode: "stereo" | "left" | "right" | "mono" | "swap";
};
```

Example: Lift the voices and play in mono

Speech around 1 kHz is 3 dB louder and both speakers play the same mixed
channel. `set` sends this plugin's whole audio chain (the nodes in order,
plus an optional `delayMs`); the player joins it with other plugins'
chains and applies it to every source (`processing.audio`,
`playback.read`, `events`).
```ts
plugin.audio.filter("sound").set({
  nodes: [
    { kind: "equalizer", frequency: 1000, q: 1, gainDb: 3 }, // +3 dB at 1 kHz
    { kind: "channels", mode: "mono" }, // both channels get (L + R) / 2
  ],
});
```

### ResolvedMedia

What a resolver returns (WebResolverOptions.resolve): the playable
stream(s) behind a page URL. Both streams must use identical `headers`;
different maps fail explicitly (nothing is dropped silently).

```ts
type ResolvedMedia = {
  /** Always `"media"`. */
  kind: "media";
  /** The page URL that was resolved. */
  originalUrl: string;
  /** A title for the player to show. */
  title?: string;
  /** The video (or combined) stream. */
  primary: ResolvedResource;
  /** A separate audio stream, when audio and video are split. */
  audio?: ResolvedResource;
};
```

Example: Play a page whose video and audio are separate streams

Opening a `https://video.example/…` page plays it with its title. When
the user opens a URL whose scheme and host a web resolver declares, the
player calls its `resolve(url, signal)`; the plugin looks up the streams
and returns them, and the player plays `primary` with the separate
`audio` track, sending the `headers` with every request for both.
```ts
plugin.resolvers.add({
  id: "video-example",
  schemes: ["https"],
  hosts: ["video.example"],
  async resolve(url, signal) {
    // The site's own API (made up here) names the streams of a page.
    const api = `https://video.example/api/streams?page=${encodeURIComponent(url)}`;
    const response = await fetch(api, { signal });
    // The player shows a failed resolve's message to the user.
    if (!response.ok)
      throw new Error(`video.example answered ${response.status} for this page`);
    const info = (await response.json()) as {
      title: string;
      video: string;
      audio: string;
    };
    const headers = { Referer: url }; // identical for both streams
    const media: ResolvedMedia = {
      kind: "media",
      originalUrl: url,
      title: info.title,
      primary: { url: info.video, headers },
      audio: { url: info.audio, headers },
    };
    return media;
  },
});
```

### SubtitleStyle

A subtitle style layer (Subtitles.setStyle). Sizes are at the
1080p reference height and scale with the video. Each plugin has one
layer; when several plugins set one, the effective style is the layer of
the plugin whose manifest id sorts last (the order of the calls does not
matter). It also applies to the secondary subtitle.

```ts
type SubtitleStyle = {
  /** A font id from SubtitlesState.fonts. */
  fontId: string;
  /** 16–72. */
  fontSize: number;
  /** Text colour. */
  color: "white" | "yellow" | "cyan";
  /** Outline width 0–4. */
  outline: number;
  /** Bottom margin 2–15 % of the video height. */
  marginPercent: number;
  /**
   * Timing offset in milliseconds, −600000…600000 (±10 minutes); positive shows the subtitles later. Outside the range the player refuses the style with `invalid`.
   */
  offsetMs: number;
  /** Bold text; default false. */
  bold?: boolean;
  /** Shadow offset 0–4 at the 1080p reference height. */
  shadow?: number;
  /** Background box opacity 0–100; `null` or omitted: no box (the shadow applies). */
  box?: number | null;
  /** `keep` (default): ASS scripts keep their own styling; `force`: this style replaces it. */
  assOverride?: "keep" | "force";
  /** Where the secondary subtitle sits; default `top`. */
  secondaryPosition?: "top" | "aboveMain";
};
```

Example: Show large yellow subtitles a quarter second earlier

Subtitles turn yellow at size 44 on a 60 % opaque box, 6 % above the
bottom of the video, and appear 250 ms earlier. `refresh` reads the
subtitle state from the player, whose `fonts` lists the font ids a style
may name; `setStyle` then sends this plugin's style layer
(`subtitles.control`, `subtitles.read`). It shows unless another plugin
with a manifest id that sorts later has a layer too: the player picks the
effective layer by manifest id, not by which call came last.
```ts
const { fonts } = await plugin.subtitles.refresh();
if (!fonts.length) return; // no font to name: leave the style alone
const style: SubtitleStyle = {
  fontId: fonts[0]!.id, // a font the player offers
  fontSize: 44, // at the 1080p reference height; scales with the video
  color: "yellow",
  outline: 2,
  marginPercent: 6, // bottom margin, % of the video height
  offsetMs: -250, // negative: shown earlier
  box: 60, // background box opacity
};
await plugin.subtitles.setStyle(style);
```

### Json

A JSON value: what crosses the wire to the player. Slint property values,
callback arguments and protocol parameters are all `Json`.

```ts
type Json = null | boolean | number | string | Json[] | {
  [key: string]: Json;
};
```

## API: @vestra-player/sdk/testing

Test tools for Vestra Player plugins: an in-memory fake player
(TestHost) and startPlugin, which activates a plugin against
it.

`TestHost` speaks the real wire protocol, so the SDK's own logic (revisions,
conditional commits, recovery after lost replies, coalescing of updates)
runs exactly as it does inside the player. Only the player side is faked,
and its semantics are simplified:

- no media decoding: sources are facts you set with
  TestHost.setSource or TestHost.openElsewhere;
- no Slint and no native windows: views are records of their properties
  and callbacks (FakeWindow), and you fire callbacks yourself;
- export jobs advance one step on every state query
  (`queued` → `running` → `completed`);
- video and audio processing nodes are validated with the player's own
  value ranges (an out-of-range `filter.set` ends in `failed` with
  `invalid`), an empty chain removes the plugin's chain, a chain on a
  generated stream fails `unsupported` (the player's own conformance
  cases check all three), and the command limits (COMMAND_LIMITS),
  property value limits (UI_VALUE_LIMITS) and menu ids
  (MENU_IDS) are enforced.

Typical workflow: start the plugin with startPlugin (it reads the
plugin's `manifest.json`), drive it the way the user or another plugin
would (run commands, press bindings, fire view callbacks, change the
source), wait with TestHost.settle, assert on what the host
recorded (`host.osd`, `host.window(id).props`, `host.sent(method)`, …), and
finally call `stop()`.

Use it from `node:test` (what `vestra-plugin test` runs). Each test should
create its own host; `stop()` removes the host's temporary directories.

### FakeWindow

A tool window as the test host keeps it: the record of a
`plugin.windows.create(...)` window after its first `show()`. Get one with
TestHost.window.

A record, not a window: no Slint file is compiled and nothing is drawn.
`props` holds what the plugin wrote, by Slint name; `emit` fires a
callback the way the user's input would; `userClose` closes it the way
the title-bar button would.

- @capability None.

```ts
interface FakeWindow {
  /** The `.slint` file the window was created from (package-relative). */
  file: string;
  /** Whether the window is shown (`show()`) or hidden (`hide()`). */
  visible: boolean;
  /**
   * The properties the plugin wrote, by their Slint (kebab-case) names: `canMark` is stored as `can-mark`. Runtime images appear in their wire form; read the path with TestHost.imagePath.
   */
  props: Record<string, Json>;
  /** The Slint callback names (kebab-case) the plugin bound with `on()`. */
  callbacks: string[];
  /**
   * Fire a Slint callback as if the user triggered it in the window. The name may be kebab-case or camelCase; `args` are the callback arguments. Follow it with `await host.settle()` before asserting.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Type into a window's search field
   * The test types "cat" into the window's search box and checks the
   * plugin's results. `emit` delivers the Slint callback `search-changed`
   * with its argument to the plugin's `on` handler; `settle()` waits for the
   * properties the handler wrote.
   * ```ts
   * const search = host.window("search");
   * search.emit("searchChanged", "cat"); // camelCase or kebab-case
   * await host.settle();
   * assert.ok((search.props["results"] as unknown[]).length > 0);
   * ```
   */
  emit(callback: string, ...args: Json[]): void;
  /**
   * The user closes the window with its title-bar button: the window closes and the plugin's `window.onClose` listeners run (unlike the plugin's own `close()`).
   * @capability None.
   * @example Close a window the way the user does
   * The test closes the plugin's window with its title-bar button and checks
   * that the plugin stopped its timer. Unlike the plugin's own `close()`,
   * `userClose` runs the plugin's `onClose` listeners.
   * ```ts
   * host.window("clock").userClose();
   * await host.settle();
   * assert.equal(host.window("clock").visible, false);
   * ```
   */
  userClose(): void;
}
```

Example: Change a setting in a tool window from a test

The test opens the plugin's Picture window, moves its brightness control
and checks that the plugin wrote the value back. `emit` fires a Slint
callback as if the user used the control; the plugin's `on` handler runs
and sets properties, which reach the host as requests, so `settle()`
waits for them before `props` is read.
```ts
await host.command("open-picture").run(); // the plugin calls window.show()
const picture = host.window("picture");
assert.equal(picture.visible, true);
picture.emit("adjust", "brightness", 40); // fire a Slint callback
await host.settle();
assert.equal(picture.props["brightness"], 40);
```

### FileDialogText

A file dialog as the player shows it (TestHost.fileDialogs).

```ts
interface FileDialogText {
  /** Which dialog. */
  kind: "openFile" | "openFiles" | "openDirectory" | "saveFile";
  /** Its title as shown, if the plugin gave one. */
  title?: string;
  /** The proposed file name as shown, if the plugin gave one. */
  fileName?: string;
}
```

### FakeCommand

A command the plugin registered with `plugin.commands.add`, as the test
host keeps it. Get one with TestHost.command (the plugin's own) or
TestHost.coreAction (the player's core actions).

The host's record of one command: what the plugin declared, the state
it last sent, and how the menu shows it in TestHost.locale.
Read it again after `settle()` to see changes; `run` executes it as the
menu would.

- @capability None.

```ts
interface FakeCommand {
  /** What the plugin declared: id, menu path, title, order, group, default bindings, focus and repeat. Wire-level shape; it may gain fields in minor versions. */
  declaration: CommandDeclaration;
  /**
   * What the menu shows, as the player shows it in the test host's TestHost.locale: the title and each path segment translated with the plugin's catalog (the player's own menus in the player's words), the keys normalized (`@video` is "Video").
   */
  readonly display: {
    /** The menu text of the item. */
    title: string;
    /** Each segment of the path as shown; empty without a path. */
    path: string[];
    /**
     * The disabled or busy reason as shown, `null` without one (a plugin command's; not enumerable, so comparing `display` with `{ title, path }` still works).
     */
    reason?: string | null;
  };
  /** The command state the player last received (after the update pass). */
  state: {
    /** `false` when the plugin disabled the command. */
    enabled: boolean;
    /** The check mark: `true`, `false`, or `null` for none. */
    checked: boolean | null;
    /** `true` while the plugin reports the command as busy. */
    busy: boolean;
    /** The reason the plugin sent (source text or a text value; see `display.reason`). */
    reason: TextValue | null;
  };
  /** The state revision the player holds; increases with every state update the SDK sends. */
  revision: number;
  /**
   * Execute the command the way the menu would, then wait until the host is idle. Rejects (with a HostError) when the command is disabled or busy, like the player, which does not call `run` then.
   * @capability None.
   * @throws command (rejects) A `HostError`: the command is disabled or busy (the message says which).
   * @example Check that a disabled item refuses to run
   * The test checks that Export cannot run while nothing is open. Like the
   * player, the host does not call `run` for a disabled or busy command;
   * the promise rejects with a `HostError`.
   * ```ts
   * await assert.rejects(host.command("export").run());
   * ```
   */
  run(): Promise<void>;
}
```

Example: Run a checkable menu item from a test

The test checks the Loop item's menu place, picks it and sees its check
mark turn on. `host.command(id)` is the host's record of what the plugin
declared and the state it last sent; `run()` calls the plugin's `run`
like the menu, after which the SDK re-evaluates the command's state and
sends it, and `run()` resolves once the host is idle again.
```ts
const toggle = host.command("toggle-loop");
assert.deepEqual(toggle.declaration.path, ["Playback", "Loop"]);
assert.equal(toggle.state.checked, false);
await toggle.run();
assert.equal(host.command("toggle-loop").state.checked, true);
```

### FakeBarButton

A command's bottom-bar button (`CommandOptions.button`) as the player shows
it: an entry of TestHost.barButtons.

A bottom-bar button as the player would show it, derived from the
command's declaration and state each time it is read: clickable while
the command is enabled and not busy, accent-coloured while checked, with
the command's title (and reason) as the tooltip.

- @capability None.

```ts
interface FakeBarButton {
  /** The command's local id. */
  readonly command: string;
  /** The icon name, or the image's path for a `plugin.ui.image` icon. */
  readonly icon: string;
  /** `true` when the icon is the plugin's image. */
  readonly image: boolean;
  /** The declared `order`. */
  readonly order: number;
  /** Clickable: the command is enabled and not busy. */
  readonly enabled: boolean;
  /** Drawn in the accent colour: the command is checked. */
  readonly checked: boolean;
  /** The tooltip without the key: the command's shown title (trailing "…" removed), then, while it cannot run, its reason on a second line. */
  readonly tooltip: string;
  /**
   * Click the button, then wait until the host is idle: runs the command as its menu item would. Rejects (with a HostError) while the button is disabled, and once the command is gone.
   * @capability None.
   * @throws command (rejects) A `HostError`: the command is disabled or busy.
   * @throws missing (rejects) A `HostError`: the command is gone.
   * @example Click the button and wait for its effect
   * The test clicks the plugin's button and checks the OSD. `click` runs the
   * command like its menu item and resolves once the host is idle.
   * ```ts
   * await host.barButtons[0]?.click();
   * assert.ok(host.osd.length > 0);
   * ```
   */
  click(): Promise<void>;
}
```

Example: Check a bar button's tooltip while it is disabled

The test checks that the Export button shows why it cannot be clicked.
The tooltip is the command's title; while the command is disabled or
busy and has a non-empty `reason`, the reason follows on a second line.
```ts
const [button] = host.barButtons;
assert.equal(button?.enabled, false);
assert.match(button?.tooltip ?? "", /\n/); // the command declares a reason
```

### FakeProducer

A generated stream (`plugin.player.openStream`) as the test host sees it:
the fake player end of the frame connection. Assertion surface; see
TestHost.producers.

The player's end of a generated stream's frame connection
(TestHost.producers): how many frames arrived and whether the
plugin released it or the player retired it. Tests assert on it; nothing
is played.

- @capability None.

```ts
interface FakeProducer {
  /** The producer id the host assigned (`1`, `2`, … per host). */
  id: number;
  /** Audio sample frames received so far (one stereo f32 pair = 1 frame). */
  receivedFrames: number;
  /** Video frames received so far. */
  videoFrames: number;
  /** `true` once the plugin released the producer (stream stopped or disposed). */
  released: boolean;
  /**
   * `true` once the player retired the producer, as the real player does at once: another source replaced it (`open`, another stream, a resolved file), the source was closed, or TestHost.failStream failed it. A retired producer's `producer.state` answers `unavailable`.
   */
  retired: boolean;
  /**
   * `true` if the frame connection closed while this stream was still the player's source: the player reports that as a playback failure ("producer transport closed"). `stop()` closes the source first.
   */
  droppedWhileSelected: boolean;
}
```

Example: Check that the stream delivers frames

The test starts the plugin's generator and checks that video and audio
arrive. The counters grow as the SDK pulls frames and sends them over
the fake connection.
```ts
await host.command("start-generator").run();
await host.settle(200); // let a few frames through
const [producer] = host.producers.values();
assert.ok((producer?.videoFrames ?? 0) > 0 && (producer?.receivedFrames ?? 0) > 0);
```

### MarkdownWire

A Markdown document as TestHost.markdown reads it back.

```ts
interface MarkdownWire {
  /** The Markdown text. */
  text: string;
  /** The base given to `ui.markdown`, or `null`. */
  base: string | null;
  /** Remote image address → the file the SDK downloaded for it. */
  images: Record<string, string>;
}
```

### TestHost

An in-memory fake Vestra Player for plugin tests.

The plugin under test talks to it over the real wire protocol (the host is
the plugin's transport), so everything the SDK does runs unchanged. The
host answers each request with simplified player behaviour, records what
the plugin did, and lets the test act as the user or another plugin.

Members fall into a few groups:

- **Drive the plugin**: TestHost.command`(id).run()`,
  TestHost.press, TestHost.window`(id).emit(...)`,
  TestHost.mounted`().emit(...)`, TestHost.drop,
  TestHost.step, TestHost.dialogAnswers.
- **Simulate the player and other plugins**: TestHost.setSource,
  TestHost.openElsewhere, TestHost.setMainWindow,
  TestHost.setTimelineLayer, TestHost.setAppearance,
  TestHost.setPackages, TestHost.emit.
- **Preset data** the plugin reads: TestHost.stats,
  TestHost.app, TestHost.systemInfo,
  TestHost.chapters, TestHost.audioDevices,
  TestHost.secrets, TestHost.clipboard,
  TestHost.tools, TestHost.rendering.
- **Assert** on records: TestHost.osd, TestHost.calls,
  TestHost.sent, TestHost.conflicts,
  TestHost.layout, TestHost.menus, and many more.
- **Inject failures**: TestHost.handle / TestHost.reset.
- **Synchronise**: TestHost.settle.

Usually created by startPlugin. Create one yourself only to preset
data that the plugin reads during activation (`app`, `appearance`,
`secrets`, ...), then pass it as `startPlugin(activate, { host })`.

Fields that mirror player state at the wire level (`source`, `subtitles`,
`processing`, `snapshots`, `jobs`, `producers`, `uploads`, `resolvers`,
`calls`) use the protocol's shapes. They are fine for assertions but are
not part of the plugin API: their shape may change in minor versions.

An in-memory player that speaks the real wire protocol, so the SDK's own
logic runs as it does in the player; only the player side is simulated
(no decoding, no Slint, no windows). Make one per test, preset it if the
plugin reads something during activation, start the plugin with
startPlugin, drive it, `settle()`, and assert on what it
recorded.

- @capability None.

```ts
class TestHost implements Transport {
  /** Every request the plugin sent, in order: `{ method, params }`. Wire-level; prefer TestHost.sent for one method. */
  readonly calls: Call[];
  /** The host events the plugin subscribed to (needs `events` etc.). */
  readonly subscriptions: Set<string>;
  /**
   * The player's source facts (phase, position, duration, paused, rate, audio tracks, loop, ...). Wire-level shape; change it with TestHost.setSource, which also broadcasts it.
   */
  source: SourceState;
  /** Tool windows by id (see TestHost.window). */
  readonly windows: Map<string, FakeWindow>;
  /** The plugin's mounted panel (bottom bar, sidebar or backdrop), or `null`. See TestHost.mounted. */
  panel: (Omit<FakeWindow, "callbacks" | "userClose"> & {
    /** `"bottom"`, `"sidebar"` or `"backdrop"`. */
    slot: string;
    /** The exported component the SDK found in the file. */
    component: string;
    /** The last `panel.setInteraction(...)` locks, `null` before any. */
    locks: Json;
  }) | null;
  /** The plugin's commands by local id (see TestHost.command). */
  readonly commands: Map<string, FakeCommand>;
  /** The player's 14 core actions (`host/<id>`), kept apart from the plugin's `commands`. */
  readonly coreCommands: Map<string, FakeCommand>;
  /**
   * Both panel positions as the player reports them (`null` while no panel is mounted there). You may change a slot directly and then call `host.emit("window.state", {})` to simulate a change made elsewhere.
   * @example Hide the sidebar and check the player's layout
   * With the plugin's panel in the sidebar, toggling the sidebar records
   * that the user prefers it hidden. `toggle()` reads the slot from the
   * player, asks for the opposite of its `preferred` flag and resolves once
   * the player answered, so the host's `layout` already shows the new value.
   * ```ts
   * assert.equal(host.layout.sidebar?.preferred, true);
   * await plugin.panels.sidebar.toggle();
   * assert.equal(host.layout.sidebar?.preferred, false);
   * ```
   */
  readonly layout: {
    /** The bottom bar position: `preferred`, `effective`, `reason`, `detached`, `owner` and `panels` (its one panel). */
    bottom: LayoutSlot | null;
    /**
     * The sidebar position: `preferred`, `effective`, `reason`, `detached`; `panels` are its tabs in order (`{ owner, plugin, title }`), `owner` the current tab's (the plugin under test is owner 1).
     */
    sidebar: LayoutSlot | null;
  };
  /**
   * Every `osd.show` text as the player shows it (translated with the plugin's catalog and formatted with its args), newest last. The template and args the plugin sent are in `host.sent("osd.show")`.
   */
  readonly osd: string[];
  /** The text of this plugin's osd panel as shown, `null` when hidden. */
  osdPanel: string | null;
  /**
   * The interface language the test host plays (`plugin.i18n.locale`), `"en"`
   * by default. Set it before startPlugin (or pass its `locale`
   * option): the plugin's catalog for it is read from the package's
   * `locales/` then, and the menus (FakeCommand.display), OSD
   * messages, dialog texts, settings page and panel titles show its
   * translations, the way the player shows them.
   *
   * The player's own texts (core actions' messages and menus, its
   * refusals) are English, or the player's Simplified Chinese for
   * `"zh-Hans"`. While `locale` was never set they stay in Chinese, as
   * players up to 0.4.2 showed them, so tests written for SDK 1.5.8 keep
   * passing; set `locale` to test what a user sees now.
   * @example Check a menu path in Simplified Chinese
   * The test starts the plugin with a Chinese interface and checks the
   * menu path its Blur item shows. The `locale` option sets
   * `host.locale` before activation, so the plugin's `locales/zh-Hans.po`
   * is loaded; the built-in menu `@video` shows in the player's own words
   * (视频), the item's title in the plugin's translation.
   * ```ts
   * const { host, stop } = await startPlugin(activate, { directory, locale: "zh-Hans" });
   * assert.deepEqual(host.command("blur").display.path, ["视频", "模糊…"]);
   * await stop();
   * ```
   */
  get locale(): Locale;
  set locale(locale: Locale);
  /**
   * Read the plugin's translations for TestHost.locale from a package directory, as the player would (`locales/<locale>.json` of a built package, else the source `locales/<locale>.po`); `startPlugin` does this. None for English; a missing file means none; a broken `.po` throws.
   * @param directory - The package directory (holding `locales/`).
   * @capability None.
   * @example Load the translations after changing the language
   * The test switches the host to German before starting the plugin and
   * loads that catalog itself (`startPlugin` does the same). Texts are then
   * shown in German.
   * ```ts
   * host.locale = "de";
   * host.loadCatalog(directory); // locales/de.po (or de.json)
   * ```
   */
  loadCatalog(directory: string): void;
  /**
   * A text of the plugin as the player shows it: translated with the plugin's catalog (TestHost.loadCatalog), then formatted with `args` when given.
   * @param text - English source text or template.
   * @param args - Values for its placeholders.
   * @returns The shown text.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Compare with a translated message
   * The test expects the text a Chinese user sees for a template the plugin
   * shows. `translate` looks the English source up in the plugin's catalog
   * for `host.locale` and fills in the arguments, the way the player does.
   * ```ts
   * assert.equal(host.translate("Speed {}×", [2]), "倍速 2×");
   * ```
   */
  translate(text: TextValue, args?: TemplateArgs): string;
  /** The saved interface language (`plugin.appearance.language`), changed by `appearance.setLanguage` or TestHost.setLanguage. */
  language: LanguagePreference;
  /**
   * Simulate another plugin (or the user) saving the interface language: pushes `appearance.changed`.
   * @param language - `"system"` or a locale.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Simulate the user choosing French for the next start
   * The plugin hears that the saved interface language changed. The host
   * pushes `appearance.changed`, which a plugin with `events` sees in
   * `appearance.language` once it has read it and subscribed; this run's
   * language does not change.
   * ```ts
   * void plugin.appearance.language; // read once: the SDK then follows it
   * plugin.appearance.onChange(() => {}); // subscribes to appearance events
   * host.setLanguage("fr");
   * await host.settle();
   * assert.equal(plugin.appearance.language, "fr");
   * ```
   */
  setLanguage(language: LanguagePreference): void;
  /**
   * Every `dialogs.confirm` as the player shows it: its texts translated (message and detail formatted with `args`), newest last. The options the plugin sent are in TestHost.confirms.
   */
  readonly confirmTexts: {
    /** The question. */
    message: string;
    /** The text under it, if any. */
    detail?: string;
    /** The confirm button. */
    confirm: string;
    /** The cancel button (the player's "Cancel" by default). */
    cancel: string;
    /** The checkbox, if any. */
    checkbox?: string;
  }[];
  /**
   * Every file dialog (`openFile`, `openFiles`, `openDirectory`, `saveFile`) as the player shows it: the title translated, a text file name translated, newest last. The options the plugin sent are in `host.sent("dialogs.open")`.
   */
  readonly fileDialogs: FileDialogText[];
  /** The sequence provider's flags, `null` without a provider. */
  sequence: {
    /** The provider's `canNext`, as last evaluated. */
    canNext: boolean;
    /** The provider's `canPrevious`, as last evaluated. */
    canPrevious: boolean;
  } | null;
  /**
   * What `player.stats()` returns. Fields added in later rounds may be left out; the SDK fills them with `null`.
   * @example Pretend a 1080p H.264 video is playing
   * The plugin's `player.stats()` now reports a 1920×1080 H.264 stream at
   * 24 fps. The host answers `stats()` with this object as it stands, so a
   * test sets it before the plugin asks; fields it leaves out come back as
   * `null` from the SDK.
   * ```ts
   * host.stats = {
   *   ...host.stats, // keep the other fields
   *   video: { codec: "h264", width: 1920, height: 1080, fps: 24 },
   * } as typeof host.stats;
   * ```
   */
  stats: PlaybackStats;
  /** Every `subtitles.load`: its options and bytes, newest last. */
  readonly subtitleLoads: {
    /** The `format` option (`"srt"` by default). */
    format: "srt" | "ass";
    /** The `title` option, `null` when omitted. */
    title: string | null;
    /** The `select` option (`"primary"` by default). */
    select: "primary" | "secondary" | "none";
    /** The uploaded file bytes. */
    bytes: Buffer;
  }[];
  /** The fake system clipboard. Preset `text` to test `readText`; `writeText` replaces it and `writeImage` appends the image path. */
  readonly clipboard: {
    /** The clipboard's text, `null` when it holds none. */
    text: string | null;
    /** Paths given to `clipboard.writeImage`, newest last. */
    images: string[];
  };
  /** The effective `power.preventSleep` mode. */
  power: "off" | "playing";
  /**
   * The fake `ffmpeg` / `ffprobe` behind `plugin.tools`. A tool without a handler is not found (`available()` is false, `run()` rejects with `unavailable`).
   * @example Fake ffprobe and a failing ffmpeg
   * The plugin's Probe command gets an empty stream list from ffprobe, and
   * any ffmpeg run fails as it would on a broken file. `handle` makes the
   * tool available and answers each `tools.run` with the handler's result;
   * a thrown `HostError` makes the run reject with that code. `calls`
   * records every run with its arguments.
   * ```ts
   * host.tools.handle("ffprobe", (args) => {
   *   assert.ok(args.includes("-show_streams")); // what the plugin asked for
   *   return { stdout: JSON.stringify({ streams: [] }) }; // a file with no streams
   * });
   * // Every ffmpeg run rejects with code `failed`.
   * host.tools.handle("ffmpeg", () => {
   *   throw new HostError("failed", "Invalid data found when processing input");
   * });
   * await host.command("probe").run();
   * assert.equal(host.tools.calls[0]?.tool, "ffprobe");
   * ```
   */
  readonly tools: {
    /** Every run: the tool name and its arguments, newest last. */
    calls: {
      /** `"ffmpeg"` or `"ffprobe"`. */
      tool: string;
      /** The arguments, as passed to `tools.run`. */
      args: string[];
    }[];
    /** @internal The installed handlers by tool; use `handle()`. */
    handlers: Map<string, (args: string[]) => {
      stdout?: Uint8Array | string;
      stderr?: string;
    } | Promise<{
      stdout?: Uint8Array | string;
      stderr?: string;
    }>>;
    /**
     * Make `tool` available and answer each run with `handler(args)`. Return `{ stdout?, stderr? }` (a string `stdout` is UTF-8 encoded), or throw a HostError to fail the run with that code. A later call replaces the handler.
     */
    handle(tool: "ffmpeg" | "ffprobe", handler: (args: string[]) => {
      stdout?: Uint8Array | string;
      stderr?: string;
    } | Promise<{
      stdout?: Uint8Array | string;
      stderr?: string;
    }>): void;
  };
