  /** Paths given to `system.reveal` / `system.openPath`, newest last; inject failures with `host.handle("system.openPath", …)`. */
  readonly system: {
    /** Paths given to `system.reveal`, newest last. */
    revealed: string[];
    /** Paths given to `system.openPath`, newest last. */
    opened: string[];
    /** `system.openUrl` addresses, newest last. */
    urls: string[];
  };
  /** Every `panel.showMenu`, newest last. */
  readonly menus: {
    /** Command ids, `null` for a separator. */
    items: (string | null)[];
    /** `at.x`, in window coordinates. */
    x: number;
    /** `at.y`, in window coordinates. */
    y: number;
  }[];
  /** Timeline layers by plugin id (this plugin's is `manifestId`) and the merged list `plugin.timeline.marks` reads. A new source clears them. */
  readonly timeline: {
    /** Each plugin's layer by plugin id; layers with no marks are absent. */
    layers: Map<string, {
      /** Seconds from the start. */
      time: number;
      /** `"chapter"`, `"bookmark"` or `"marker"`. */
      kind: string;
      /** The mark's title, `null` without one. */
      title: string | null;
    }[]>;
    /** Every layer merged, sorted by time, with the publishing plugin's id. */
    readonly marks: {
      /** The manifest id of the plugin that published the mark. */
      plugin: string;
      /** Seconds from the start. */
      time: number;
      /** `"chapter"`, `"bookmark"` or `"marker"`. */
      kind: string;
      /** The mark's title, `null` without one. */
      title: string | null;
    }[];
  };
  /**
   * Simulate another plugin publishing its timeline layer (or clearing it with `[]`); pushes `timeline.changed` when the plugin subscribed.
   * @param pluginId - The other plugin's manifest id.
   * @param marks - Its whole layer.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Let another plugin publish chapters
   * The plugin under test sees two chapter marks another plugin put on the
   * timeline. `setTimelineLayer` stores that plugin's whole layer and pushes
   * `timeline.changed`; once the plugin uses `plugin.timeline` (with
   * `events`) the SDK keeps `marks` current from that event, and `settle()`
   * lets it arrive.
   * ```ts
   * host.setTimelineLayer("community.chapters", [
   *   { time: 0, kind: "chapter", title: "Intro" },
   *   { time: 95, kind: "chapter", title: "Part 1" },
   * ]); // replaces that plugin's whole layer; [] would clear it
   * await host.settle();
   * assert.equal(plugin.timeline.marks.length, 2);
   * ```
   */
  setTimelineLayer(pluginId: string, marks: {
    time: number;
    kind: string;
    title?: string | null;
  }[]): void;
  /**
   * Runtime images written to views (`plugin.ui.image`, `plugin.ui.remoteImage`), whole values and (SDK 1.5.19) images nested in rows, newest last. The SDK refuses images of released scopes before anything is sent. The test host does not read the files, so it does not check the player's per-view budget (`IMAGE_LIMITS.viewBytes`).
   */
  readonly images: {
    /** The image file's path, as given to `ui.image`. */
    path: string;
    /** The SDK's reference number for that `ImageRef`. */
    ref: number;
    /** Its `maxSide` option, when given. */
    maxSide?: number;
  }[];
  /**
   * The file an image property shows, or `null` when the value is not a runtime image. View properties hold images in their wire form; this reads the path back.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Check which file a window shows as its cover
   * The test checks that the Cover window's image comes from the plugin's
   * data directory. An image property holds the SDK's wire form of
   * `plugin.ui.image(path)`, not a path; `imagePath` reads the path back.
   * ```ts
   * assert.equal(
   *   host.imagePath(host.window("cover").props["cover"]),
   *   join(plugin.dataDirectory, "cover.png"),
   * );
   * ```
   */
  imagePath(value: Json | undefined): string | null;
  /** `drops.provide` registrations of this plugin, in order (`id` is the SDK's). */
  readonly dropProviders: {
    /** The SDK's provider id. */
    id: string;
    /** The extensions it takes (lower case, `"folder"` for directories). */
    extensions: string[];
  }[];
  /** The panel has an `onDrop` listener. */
  panelDrops: boolean;
  /**
   * Drop files like the player: on a panel with an `onDrop` listener the whole list goes there; otherwise (and on the video area) each path goes to the first provider of its extension (`folder` for existing directories), one call per provider with all of its paths. Files nobody takes are ignored. Resolves once the host is idle again.
   * @param paths - The dropped paths, in the order the file manager gives.
   * @param options - `target`: `"video"` (default) or `"panel"`; `at`: the drop point in panel coordinates (default `{ x: 0, y: 0 }`); `modifiers`: keys held (default all `false`).
   * @capability None.
   * @throws Never: files nobody takes are ignored, as in the player.
   * @example Drop files on the video and on the panel
   * The first drop lands on the video area: each extension belongs to the
   * provider that registered it first, and each provider gets one call with
   * all of its paths. The second lands on the panel at a point, with Alt
   * held, and the panel's `onDrop` gets the whole list. `drop` resolves
   * once the host is idle.
   * ```ts
   * await host.drop(["/media/a.srt", "/media/b.mkv"]); // on the video area
   * // On the panel, 10 px from its left and 48 px from its top, Alt held.
   * await host.drop(["/media/list.m3u"], {
   *   target: "panel",
   *   at: { x: 10, y: 48 },
   *   modifiers: { alt: true },
   * });
   * ```
   */
  drop(paths: string[], options?: {
    target?: "video" | "panel";
    at?: {
      x: number;
      y: number;
    };
    modifiers?: Partial<{
      alt: boolean;
      shift: boolean;
      cmd: boolean;
    }>;
  }): Promise<void>;
  /** The palette (`plugin.appearance.theme`); `setAppearance` changes it elsewhere. */
  appearance: ThemeId;
  /**
   * Simulate another plugin switching the palette: updates TestHost.appearance and pushes `appearance.changed`.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Simulate another plugin switching to the light palette
   * The plugin hears the palette change. The host updates `appearance` and
   * pushes `appearance.changed` to a plugin that listens with `events`.
   * ```ts
   * const themes: ThemeId[] = [];
   * plugin.appearance.onChange((theme) => themes.push(theme)); // subscribes (`events`)
   * host.setAppearance("vestra-light");
   * await host.settle();
   * assert.deepEqual(themes, ["vestra-light"]);
   * ```
   */
  setAppearance(theme: ThemeId): void;
  /** Settings pages by id (`plugin.settings.page`), every `show` (page id or null), and the page the options window shows. */
  readonly settings: {
    /** Registered pages by page id. */
    pages: Map<string, {
      /** The page's settings category. */
      category: string;
      /** The page title. */
      title: string;
      /** The page order within its category. */
      order: number;
      /** The `.slint` file (package-relative). */
      file: string;
      /** The exported component the SDK found. */
      component: string;
      /** The exported global (the page's bridge) the SDK found. */
      global: string;
      /** The page's properties by Slint (kebab-case) name. */
      props: Record<string, Json>;
      /** Fire one of the page's callbacks. */
      emit(callback: string, ...args: Json[]): void;
    }>;
    /** Every `settings.show(pageId)`: the page id, `null` when omitted. */
    shows: (string | null)[];
    /** The page the options window shows, `null` before any `show`. */
    current: string | null;
    /** Whether the options window is open. */
    open: boolean;
  };
  /**
   * One settings page by id. Throws when it was never registered.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Change a value on the plugin's settings page
   * The test sets the step on the General page and checks the page shows
   * it. `emit` fires the page's callback as the user's input would; the
   * plugin's handler stores the value and its `bind` function sends it back
   * as a property, which `settle()` waits for.
   * ```ts
   * const page = host.settingsPage("general");
   * page.emit("setStep", 10);
   * await host.settle();
   * assert.equal(page.props["step"], 10);
   * ```
   */
  settingsPage(id: string): {
    /** The page's settings category. */
    category: string;
    /** The page title. */
    title: string;
    /** The page order within its category. */
    order: number;
    /** The `.slint` file (package-relative). */
    file: string;
    /** The exported component the SDK found. */
    component: string;
    /** The exported global (the page's bridge) the SDK found. */
    global: string;
    /** The page's properties by Slint (kebab-case) name. */
    props: Record<string, Json>;
    /** Fire one of the page's callbacks. */
    emit(callback: string, ...args: Json[]): void;
  };
  /** The backdrop: who mounted it and whether it shows (`panels.backdrop.state`). */
  backdrop: {
    /** The manifest id of the plugin that mounted it. */
    owner: string;
    /** Whether it shows now (no video frame). `true` when mounted. */
    effective: boolean;
  } | null;
  /**
   * Simulate the backdrop's `effective` changing (`false`: a video frame appeared; `true`: there is none again); pushed to the plugin.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Make a video picture replace the backdrop
   * The plugin's backdrop hears that a video frame now covers it. `false`
   * means a picture appeared; the change is pushed like the player's
   * `window.state`.
   * ```ts
   * host.setBackdropEffective(false);
   * await host.settle();
   * assert.equal(plugin.panels.backdrop.state?.effective, false);
   * ```
   */
  setBackdropEffective(effective: boolean): void;
  /**
   * Simulate another plugin mounting a panel, before or after the plugin under test, as the player handles it: in the sidebar it is another tab (after the existing ones; the first panel's tab is current); the bottom bar and the backdrop take one panel, so the plugin's own mount there then rejects with `conflict` (not an activation failure, as in the player). Pushed as a `window.state` change.
   * @param slot - The position.
   * @param plugin - The other plugin's manifest id.
   * @param options - `title`: its tab label (default: `plugin`).
   * @capability None.
   * @example Put the playlist next to this plugin's sidebar panel
   * The sidebar ends up with two tabs: the playlist, mounted first, and the
   * plugin's own panel after it. `mountOther` before `startPlugin` mounts
   * another plugin's panel as the player would, so the plugin's mount
   * during activation becomes the second tab (in the bottom bar or the
   * backdrop it would be refused with `conflict` instead).
   * ```ts
   * const host = new TestHost();
   * host.mountOther("sidebar", "vestra.playlist", { title: "播放列表" });
   * await startPlugin(activate, { host, directory });
   * assert.equal(host.layout.sidebar?.panels?.length, 2);
   * ```
   */
  mountOther(slot: "bottom" | "sidebar" | "backdrop", plugin: string, options?: {
    title?: string;
  }): void;
  /**
   * Simulate another plugin's panel going away (TestHost.mountOther): when its tab was current, the next tab (else the previous one) is.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Let the playlist's tab go away
   * The other plugin's sidebar tab disappears and the plugin's own tab
   * becomes current. When the removed tab was current, the next tab (else
   * the previous one) becomes current, as in the player.
   * ```ts
   * host.unmountOther("vestra.playlist");
   * await host.settle();
   * assert.equal(host.layout.sidebar?.panels?.length, 1);
   * ```
   */
  unmountOther(plugin: string): void;
  /**
   * Simulate the user clicking a sidebar tab: `plugin`'s panel (the plugin under test's `manifestId`, or one of TestHost.mountOther) becomes the current tab. Pushed as a `window.state` change.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Click another plugin's sidebar tab
   * The user switches the sidebar to the playlist; the plugin's panel is in
   * a background tab now. The change is pushed as `window.state`.
   * ```ts
   * host.selectTab("vestra.playlist");
   * await host.settle();
   * assert.notEqual(host.layout.sidebar?.owner, 1); // the plugin under test is owner 1
   * ```
   */
  selectTab(plugin: string): void;
  /** The display layer (`plugin.video.view()`): who owns it (this plugin is `manifestId`) and the values the player holds. */
  readonly videoView: {
    /** The owning plugin's manifest id, `null` while nobody owns it. */
    owner: string | null;
    /** The values the player holds. */
    values: ViewSettings;
  };
  /**
   * Simulate another plugin taking the display layer first (the plugin's `video.view()` then fails with `conflict`), or, with `null`, releasing it (values reset to the defaults).
   * @capability None.
   * @example Let another plugin own the display layer
   * The plugin's `video.view()` fails with `conflict` because another plugin
   * took the display layer first. `null` releases it again.
   * ```ts
   * host.setVideoViewOwner("someone.zoom");
   * const view = plugin.video.view();
   * view.set({ zoom: 2 });
   * await host.settle();
   * assert.equal(view.status.state, "failed");
   * ```
   */
  setVideoViewOwner(pluginId: string | null): void;
  /**
   * The render options (`plugin.video.render()`): who owns them, the values the player holds, and whether it renders on the GPU (`gpu: false` is software rendering, where every `set` fails with `unsupported`).
   */
  readonly videoRender: {
    /** The owning plugin's manifest id, `null` while nobody owns them. */
    owner: string | null;
    /** The values the player holds. */
    values: RenderSettings;
    /** `true`: GPU rendering; `false`: software rendering (`unsupported`). `plugin.app.system()` reports it as `rendering`. */
    gpu: boolean;
  };
  /**
   * Simulate another plugin owning the render options (the plugin's `video.render()` then fails with `conflict`), or, with `null`, releasing them (values reset to the defaults).
   * @capability None.
   * @example Let another plugin own the render options
   * The plugin's render options report `conflict` while another plugin owns
   * them; `null` releases them and resets the values to the defaults.
   * ```ts
   * host.setVideoRenderOwner("someone.hdr");
   * const render = plugin.video.render();
   * render.set({ toneMapping: "bt.2390" });
   * await host.settle();
   * assert.equal(render.status.state, "failed");
   * ```
   */
  setVideoRenderOwner(pluginId: string | null): void;
  /**
   * What the player pushes when mpv cannot compile a shader (code `failed`) or switches to software rendering (`unsupported`, which also sets `videoRender.gpu` to false and `rendering.reason` to `window-fallback` with `message`). Pushed only when this plugin is the owner.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Make a shader fail to compile
   * The plugin's render options report `failed`, as when mpv rejects a
   * shader. The host pushes the failure only while this plugin owns the
   * render options, which its first accepted `set` made it; the SDK updates
   * the handle's `status` when the push arrives, so the test settles first.
   * ```ts
   * const render = plugin.video.render();
   * render.set({ toneMapping: "bt.2390" }); // makes the plugin the owner
   * await host.settle();
   * host.failVideoRender("failed", "shader compile failed: ERROR: 0:39: ...");
   * await host.settle();
   * assert.equal(render.status.state, "failed");
   * ```
   */
  failVideoRender(code: "failed" | "unsupported", message: string): void;
  /**
   * The player's processing (filter) state. Wire-level; may change in minor versions. `resources` holds each `video.filter` / `audio.filter` chain the plugin applied, keyed by the SDK's resource id.
   * @example Check the filter chain the plugin applied
   * After the plugin set its picture chain, the test reads the one chain
   * the host holds and compares its nodes. `resources` keeps each applied
   * `video.filter` / `audio.filter` chain by the SDK's resource id, after
   * the host validated it with the player's value ranges.
   * ```ts
   * const [chain] = [...host.processing.resources.values()];
   * assert.deepEqual(chain?.nodes, [{ kind: "hue", degrees: 30 }]);
   * ```
   */
  readonly processing: {
    /** Increases with every accepted change. */
    configurationRevision: number;
    /** Set a stage here to simulate a blocked backend (`backend-uncertain`). */
    backendUncertain: Partial<Record<"video" | "audio", string>>;
    /** Applied chains by resource id; an empty chain removes its entry, as in the player. */
    resources: Map<string, {
      /** `"video"` or `"audio"`. */
      stage: string;
      /** The chain's revision. */
      revision: number;
      /** The applied nodes. */
      nodes: Json;
      /** The audio delay in milliseconds (audio chains only). */
      offsetMs?: number;
    }>;
    /** Outcomes of processing operations, for the SDK's recovery queries. */
    book: Map<string, {
      /** The operation's outcome. */
      status: "completed" | "failed";
      /** The result of a completed operation. */
      result?: Json;
      /** The refusal of a failed operation. */
      error?: {
        /** The error code. */
        code: string;
        /** The error message. */
        message: string;
      };
    }>;
  };
  /**
   * The player's subtitle state: tracks, selection, style layers, fonts and loaded resources. Wire-level shape (may change in minor versions); add tracks to `subtitles.tracks` (entries may carry `codec`, `text`, `streamIndex`) to simulate a source's subtitles.
   */
  subtitles: SubtitleState;
  /** Subtitle uploads in progress, by upload id. Wire-level. */
  readonly uploads: Map<number, {
    /** The chunks received so far. */
    bytes: Buffer[];
    /** The announced total size in bytes. */
    expected: number;
    /** The source generation it was begun for; like the player, a new source drops the uploads of the old one. */
    generation?: number;
  }>;
  /** Snapshots taken with `media.capture`, by snapshot id. Wire-level. */
  readonly snapshots: Map<number, Json>;
  /** Every `jobs.start` request (`kind`, `destination`, `quality`, …), newest last. */
  readonly exports: Record<string, Json>[];
  /** Export jobs by job id. Each state query advances a job one step (`queued` → `running` → `completed`; `cancelling` → `cancelled`). Wire-level. */
  readonly jobs: Map<number, MediaJob>;
  /**
   * `openStream`'s transport: a local stream (a Unix socket on macOS and Linux, a named pipe on Windows) or, with `"tcp"`, loopback TCP where the plugin must send the token first, as the player on Windows answers. Set it before the plugin calls `openStream`.
   */
  producerTransport: "unix" | "tcp";
  /** Generated streams (`player.openStream`) by producer id: the fake player end of each frame connection. Wire-level beyond the FakeProducer fields. */
  readonly producers: Map<number, FakeProducer & {
    /** The listening server for the frame connection. */
    server: Server;
    /** The Unix socket path (unused with TCP). */
    path: string;
    /** TCP: the connection sent the right token (always true for Unix). */
    admitted: boolean;
    /** The current start/stop control epoch. */
    epoch: number;
    /** A control waiting for the plugin's acknowledgement, or `null`. */
    pending: Json | null;
    /** Whether the last control was acknowledged. */
    acknowledged: boolean;
    /** Whether the stream is producing (selected and started). */
    active: boolean;
  }>;
  /** Registered source resolvers (`resolvers.add`) by id: their declarations. */
  readonly resolvers: Map<string, Json>;
  /**
   * Resolvers other plugins hold, as `resolvers.add` declares them plus the holder's id: a registration of this plugin that claims one of their extensions (or scheme + host pairs) is refused with `conflict`, which does not fail activation, like the player.
   * @example Start with another plugin holding a file type
   * The plugin starts in a player where another plugin already resolves
   * `.ch8` files. Pushed before `startPlugin`, the entry makes the plugin's
   * own resolver for `.ch8` fail with `conflict` during activation, which
   * (as in the player) does not fail the activation.
   * ```ts
   * const host = new TestHost();
   * host.otherResolvers.push({ owner: "example.emulator", extensions: ["ch8"] });
   * ```
   */
  readonly otherResolvers: {
    /** The manifest id of the plugin holding them (shown in the refusal). */
    owner: string;
    /** File extensions it resolves (a file resolver), lower case, no dot. */
    extensions?: string[];
    /** URL schemes it resolves (a web resolver), with `hosts`. */
    schemes?: string[];
    /** Exact host names it resolves (a web resolver), with `schemes`. */
    hosts?: string[];
  }[];
  /**
   * What `plugin.resolvers.fileTypes` reports: the extensions of this plugin's file resolvers and of TestHost.otherResolvers, sorted, each once.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Check the file types a resolver adds
   * The test checks the list the plugin will read as
   * `resolvers.fileTypes`: the extensions of its own file resolvers and of
   * `otherResolvers`, sorted, each once.
   * ```ts
   * assert.deepEqual(host.fileTypes(), ["ch8"]);
   * ```
   */
  fileTypes(): string[];
  /**
   * Push `resolvers.fileTypes` when TestHost.fileTypes changed: called after this plugin's resolvers come and go; call it yourself after changing TestHost.otherResolvers (another plugin started or stopped).
   * @capability None.
   * @example Let another plugin's file type appear while running
   * Another plugin starts and adds `.ch8`; the plugin under test then sees
   * it in `resolvers.fileTypes`. Changing `otherResolvers` alone pushes
   * nothing: `updateFileTypes` sends the new list as the player does when
   * a plugin starts or stops, and `settle()` lets the SDK apply it.
   * ```ts
   * host.otherResolvers.push({ owner: "example.emulator", extensions: ["ch8"] });
   * host.updateFileTypes();
   * await host.settle();
   * assert.deepEqual(plugin.resolvers.fileTypes, ["ch8"]);
   * ```
   */
  updateFileTypes(): void;
  /**
   * File opens waiting for this plugin's file resolver (`extensions`), by request id: the path and how it was opened. Opening a matching path (`player.open`, TestHost.openElsewhere) sends `source.resolveRequest`; the answer selects the stream, fails the open or, once the source changed, is `stale`. Any later source change cancels it (`source.resolveCancel`). Web resolvers are not simulated: emit `source.resolveRequest` yourself.
   */
  readonly resolutions: Map<number, {
    /** The id of this plugin's resolver asked (`resolvers.add` `id`). */
    resolverId: string;
    /** The path being opened, as sent to `resolve`. */
    source: string;
    /** The open asked for a paused start (`player.open(path, { paused })`). */
    paused: boolean;
  }>;
  /**
   * Answers for `dialogs.open` (paths, `null` = cancelled) and
   * `dialogs.confirm` (`{ confirmed, checked }`), consumed in order. A
   * dialog with no queued answer, or with the wrong kind, fails the request
   * (as a lost reply).
   *
   * For `openFile` / `openDirectory` / `saveFile` queue a one-path array;
   * for `openFiles` any number of paths.
   * @example Answer the plugin's dialogs in advance
   * The plugin's Open command gets a picked file, then a cancelled file
   * dialog, then a confirmed question. All answers share one queue, taken
   * from the front in the order the plugin opens dialogs of any kind: if
   * the next queued answer is missing or of the wrong kind, the dialog
   * fails like a lost reply, so queue them in the order the plugin asks.
   * ```ts
   * host.dialogAnswers.push(["/media/movie.mkv"]); // openFile picks it
   * host.dialogAnswers.push(null); // the next file dialog is cancelled
   * host.dialogAnswers.push({ confirmed: true, checked: false }); // confirm
   * await host.command("open").run();
   * ```
   */
  readonly dialogAnswers: (string[] | null | {
    /** The user clicked the confirm button. */
    confirmed: boolean;
    /** The checkbox state. */
    checked: boolean;
  })[];
  /** Every `dialogs.confirm` request (its options), newest last. */
  readonly confirms: Record<string, Json>[];
  /**
   * The main window as the player would show it. Change it with `setMainWindow` (the user resized it, entered fullscreen, closed the picture-in-picture window); `onTop`, `cursorAutoHide` and `pictureInPicture.active` record the plugin's `window.set…` calls. `pictureInPicture.supported: false` stands for Windows and Linux.
   */
  readonly mainWindow: {
    /** Whether the main window is fullscreen. */
    fullscreen: boolean;
    /** The video area in logical points (default 780×609). */
    videoArea: {
      /** Width in logical points. */
      width: number;
      /** Height in logical points. */
      height: number;
    };
    /** The effective `window.setAlwaysOnTop` value. */
    onTop: boolean;
    /** The effective `window.setCursorAutoHide` mode. */
    cursorAutoHide: "fullscreen" | "playing";
    /** Picture-in-picture: `supported` (preset) and `active`. */
    pictureInPicture: {
      /** Set to `false` to simulate Windows or Linux. */
      supported: boolean;
      /** Whether the picture-in-picture window shows the video. */
      active: boolean;
    };
  };
  /**
   * The player's secret store for this plugin: name → value. Preset entries to simulate stored secrets; inject failures with `host.handle("secrets.get", ...)`. Like the player, `secrets.set` of a new name fails `limit` once 256 names are stored.
   */
  readonly secrets: Map<string, string>;
  /**
   * `plugin.storage.session`: key → value, as the player keeps them. Preset entries to simulate values an earlier run of the plugin stored in the same player session, or pass `startPlugin(..., { sessionStorage })`. Like the player, a key is 1–1024 bytes, a `set` that would make the entries larger than 1 MiB (keys, values as compact JSON and `SESSION_STORAGE_LIMITS.entryBytes` per key) fails `limit`, and an object's properties are stored sorted, as the player hands them back.
   */
  readonly sessionStorage: Map<string, Json>;
  /**
   * What `plugin.app.system()` reports. Its `rendering` follows videoRender.gpu (`"gpu"` or `"software"`), so one switch covers the render options and the fact; its `renderingReason` is rendering.reason.
   */
  systemInfo: Omit<WireSystemInfo, "rendering" | "renderingReason">;
  /** What `plugin.app` reports. Set it before startPlugin: the plugin receives it once at start-up. */
  app: {
    /** The player version. */
    version: string;
    /** The short git hash of the build, `null` when unknown. */
    build: string | null;
    /** Component versions. */
    components: {
      /** libmpv's `mpv-version`. */
      mpv: string | null;
      /** `{ ffmpeg: <version> }`. */
      libav: Record<string, string>;
      /** The Slint version. */
      slint: string;
    };
  };
  /**
   * The player's rendering choice behind `plugin.rendering` (player
   * 0.5.13). The mode drawing now is videoRender.gpu, as for `plugin.app.system()`; the rest is preset here
   * and changed by the plugin's calls, as the player would:
   *
   * - `setPreference` saves `preference` and never changes the mode. It
   *   refuses `"gpu"` while `gpu.available` is false: with `unsupported`
   *   when `gpu.reason.code` is `no-gpu-backend` or `headless`, otherwise
   *   with `unavailable`, the reason's message in both cases.
   * - The next start uses `"software"` for the `"software"` choice, else
   *   software with `gpu.reason` while the GPU is not available, else the
   *   GPU (code `preference` for a `"gpu"` choice, `default` for
   *   `"auto"`). `restartPending` compares that with `startedWith`.
   * - `restartPlayer` counts in `restarts` and leaves the plugin running
   *   (call `stop()` yourself); a second one rejects with `busy`, as a
   *   restart is then under way.
   *
   * Inject other refusals (`failed` for an unwritable settings file or a
   * new process that could not start) with `host.handle("rendering.setPreference", …)`
   * or `host.handle("rendering.restart", …)`. The defaults are a macOS
   * player on the GPU: `"auto"`, available, started on the GPU.
   * @example Test a GPU switch on a system without a GPU renderer
   * The plugin's GPU menu item is greyed out with the player's reason when
   * the GPU cannot be chosen. The host is preset before the plugin starts,
   * because the plugin reads the state while activating; software
   * rendering is `videoRender.gpu = false`, and `gpu` says why the GPU
   * cannot be chosen.
   * ```ts
   * import assert from "node:assert/strict";
   * import { startPlugin, TestHost } from "@vestra-player/sdk/testing";
   * import activate from "../main.ts";
   *
   * const host = new TestHost();
   * host.videoRender.gpu = false; // software draws now (Windows)
   * host.rendering.startedWith = "software";
   * host.rendering.reason = { code: "no-gpu-backend", message: "No GPU renderer on Windows" };
   * host.rendering.gpu = { available: false, reason: host.rendering.reason };
   * const { stop } = await startPlugin(activate, {
   *   directory: new URL("..", import.meta.url),
   *   host,
   * });
   * const item = host.command("gpu-rendering");
   * assert.equal(item.state.enabled, false);
   * assert.equal(item.state.reason, "No GPU renderer on Windows");
   * await stop();
   * ```
   */
  readonly rendering: {
    /** Why the mode drawing now is what it is (`RenderingState.reason`, `SystemInfo.renderingReason`). */
    reason: RenderingReason;
    /** The saved choice: `"auto"`, `"gpu"` or `"software"`. */
    preference: RenderingPreference;
    /** The mode this run started with; `restartPending` compares the next start's mode with it. */
    startedWith: RenderingMode;
    /** Whether the plugin may choose `"gpu"`, and why not (`null` while available). */
    gpu: {
      /** `false`: `setPreference("gpu")` is refused. */
      available: boolean;
      /** Why the GPU cannot be chosen; `null` while it can. */
      reason: RenderingReason | null;
    };
    /** Accepted `restartPlayer` calls. */
    restarts: number;
  };
  /** What `player.chapters()` lists while media is ready. */
  chapters: {
    /** The chapter title, `null` without one. */
    title: string | null;
    /** Start time in seconds. */
    start: number;
  }[];
  /**
   * `plugin.dataDirectory`: a fresh empty temporary directory, removed with the host on `stop()`. `plugin.storage.json` reads and writes real files here. Pass `startPlugin(..., { dataDirectory })` to use another one.
   */
  readonly dataDirectory: string;
  /** The manifest id of the plugin under test (set by startPlugin; `"test.plugin"` by default). */
  manifestId: string;
  /**
   * A fresh in-memory player: nothing open, no plugin, the player's core actions registered. Preset what the plugin reads during activation, then pass it to startPlugin as `host`.
   */
  constructor();
  /** The `player.setStepSeek` value in effect (default 5). */
  stepSeek: number;
  /** The `player.setStepSeek` `keyframes` in effect (default `false`, SDK 1.5.19). */
  stepSeekKeyframes: boolean;
  /**
   * Test data: the keyframe times (seconds, ascending) of the current source, for keyframe step seeks. `null` (the default): none modelled, and step seeks are exact even with `stepSeekKeyframes`.
   * @example Step forward to the next keyframe
   * With keyframe step seeks on, Forward from 0:12 lands on the keyframe at
   * 0:20, not at 0:17, and the OSD says so. `keyframes` gives the source's
   * keyframe times; `setStepSeek` turns on keyframe steps of 5 s, and the
   * core action `seek-forward` seeks to the first keyframe at or after
   * the target, as the player does.
   * ```ts
   * host.setSource({ phase: "ready", duration: 45, position: 12 });
   * host.keyframes = [0, 10, 20, 30, 40];
   * await plugin.player.setStepSeek({ seconds: 5, keyframes: true });
   * await plugin.host.run("seek-forward"); // target 17 s, next keyframe 20 s
   * assert.equal(host.source.position, 20);
   * assert.equal(host.osd.at(-1), "Forward 5 s: 00:20 / 00:45");
   * ```
   */
  keyframes: number[] | null;
  /**
   * Every step seek the core ran (`seek-backward` / `seek-forward`, from a key, the menu or `host.run`), newest last: the step, whether it went to a keyframe, and where it landed.
   */
  readonly coreSeeks: {
    /** `seek-backward` or `seek-forward`. */
    action: string;
    /** The step: `host.run`'s `seconds`, else `setStepSeek`'s. */
    seconds: number;
    /** It landed on a keyframe (`stepSeekKeyframes` and keyframes modelled). */
    keyframes: boolean;
    /** The new position. */
    landed: number;
  }[];
  /**
   * Every seek a plugin submitted (`player.seek`, `Scrub.seek`), newest last, with the mode it asked for. The test host lands on the exact target either way (the player lands a `keyframes` seek on the last keyframe at or before it); the core's step seeks are in `coreSeeks`.
   */
  readonly seeks: {
    /** The target. */
    seconds: number;
    /** `Scrub.seek(seconds, { keyframes: true })` (SDK 1.5.22). */
    keyframes: boolean;
  }[];
  /** Every `player.step`, newest last. */
  readonly steps: {
    /** `"frame"` or `"keyframe"`. */
    unit: string;
    /** `"backward"` or `"forward"`. */
    direction: string;
  }[];
  /** Every core action run (`host.run`, a core command, a pressed core binding), newest last. */
  readonly coreRuns: string[];
  /**
   * One of the 14 core actions (`play-pause`, `stop`, `seek-forward`, ...) that the test host registers like the player, as `host/<id>`. Throws for an unknown id. `run()` executes it like its menu item: a disabled action rejects with `command`, as in the player (`plugin.host.run` rejects with `unavailable` instead); otherwise it runs with the player's checks and writes its on-screen text to TestHost.osd.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Pause through the player's own action
   * The test pauses playback the way the Space key does and checks that the
   * host recorded it. Core actions belong to the player (`host/<id>`);
   * `run()` applies the player's checks, so a source must be ready first,
   * and every run is appended to `coreRuns`.
   * ```ts
   * host.setSource({ phase: "ready", duration: 100, position: 10 });
   * await host.coreAction("play-pause").run();
   * assert.equal(host.source.paused, true);
   * assert.deepEqual(host.coreRuns, ["play-pause"]);
   * ```
   */
  coreAction(id: string): FakeCommand;
  /**
   * Replace the host's behaviour for one wire method until
   * TestHost.reset. The handler receives the request parameters and
   * returns the reply (or a promise of it).
   *
   * Throw a HostError to simulate a definite refusal (the plugin's
   * call rejects with that `code`); throw a plain `Error` to simulate a lost
   * reply (the SDK then runs its recovery path). Method names are protocol
   * names, e.g. `"clipboard.writeText"`, `"secrets.get"`,
   * `"system.openPath"`, `"audio.addTrack"`; see TestHost.sent to
   * find the one a call uses.
   * @param method - The wire method name.
   * @param handler - Produces the reply from the request parameters.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Make opening a folder fail
   * The plugin's Open Folder command meets a missing folder and must tell
   * the user. `handle` replaces the host's answer to one wire method; the
   * `HostError` it throws reaches the plugin as a rejection with code
   * `missing`, like the player's refusal. `reset` restores the default
   * behaviour for the rest of the test.
   * ```ts
   * host.handle("system.openPath", () => {
   *   throw new HostError("missing", "no such file");
   * });
   * await host.command("open-folder").run(); // the plugin catches `missing`
   * assert.deepEqual(host.osd, ["Folder not found"]);
   * host.reset("system.openPath");
   * ```
   */
  handle(method: string, handler: Handler): void;
  /**
   * Restore the default behaviour of a method replaced with TestHost.handle.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Restore the default answer after a simulated failure
   * The first write fails, the second succeeds. `reset` removes the handler
   * that `handle` installed, so the method is answered by the test host
   * again.
   * ```ts
   * host.handle("clipboard.writeText", () => {
   *   throw new HostError("failed", "denied");
   * });
   * await assert.rejects(plugin.clipboard.writeText("x"));
   * host.reset("clipboard.writeText");
   * await plugin.clipboard.writeText("x"); // the default handler again
   * ```
   */
  reset(method: string): void;
  /**
   * Deliver a host event to the plugin. Like the player, subscription-based events (`source.state`, `playback.backend`, `window.state`, `timeline.changed`, `appearance.changed`) are delivered only when the plugin subscribed (it declared `events` and listens). Most tests use the higher-level helpers (`setSource`, `setMainWindow`, ...) instead.
   * @param event - The wire event name.
   * @param data - The event payload (wire-level shape).
   * @capability None.
   * @example Deliver a raw event the helpers do not cover
   * The test pushes a `window.state` event after changing `layout` by hand.
   * Like the player, the host delivers it only when the plugin subscribed;
   * most tests use `setSource`, `setMainWindow` and the other helpers
   * instead.
   * ```ts
   * host.emit("window.state", {}); // no facts: the SDK reads window.state again
   * await host.settle();
   * ```
   */
  emit(event: string, data: unknown): void;
  /**
   * Change the source facts and broadcast them, as if the player's state changed (the user paused, playback reached the end, a file finished loading). Any phase other than `empty` also turns on the source capabilities (pause, seek, rate, ...) unless the patch sets them. `phase: "loading"` makes a mounted backdrop effective, like the player.
   * @param patch - Wire-level source fields, e.g. `phase`, `position`, `duration`, `paused`, `audioTracks`.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Load a file, then let it play to the end
   * The plugin sees a one-minute source become ready, then end on its own.
   * `setSource` changes the host's source facts and broadcasts them like
   * the player's events; the SDK updates `player.state` when the event
   * arrives, so the test settles before reading it.
   * ```ts
   * host.setSource({ phase: "ready", duration: 60, position: 0 });
   * await host.settle();
   * assert.equal(plugin.player.state.phase, "ready");
   * host.setSource({ phase: "ended", terminalReason: "natural" });
   * await host.settle();
   * ```
   */
  setSource(patch: Partial<SourceState>): void;
  /**
   * Simulate the user changing the main window (resizing it, entering or leaving fullscreen, closing the picture-in-picture window) and broadcast it. Like the player, entering fullscreen collapses an attached, visible sidebar (`effective: false`, `reason: "fullscreen"`) and leaving fullscreen docks it again.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Go fullscreen, then report picture-in-picture support
   * The plugin sees the main window fullscreen at 1920×1080, then learns
   * that picture-in-picture is available. `setMainWindow` changes the
   * host's window facts and broadcasts them as the player does when the
   * user resizes or toggles fullscreen; entering fullscreen also collapses
   * an attached sidebar.
   * ```ts
   * host.setMainWindow({ fullscreen: true, videoArea: { width: 1920, height: 1080 } });
   * await host.settle();
   * assert.equal(plugin.window.state.fullscreen, true);
   * host.setMainWindow({ pictureInPicture: { supported: true, active: false } });
   * ```
   */
  setMainWindow(patch: Partial<{
    fullscreen: boolean;
    videoArea: {
      width: number;
      height: number;
    };
    pictureInPicture: {
      supported: boolean;
      active: boolean;
    };
  }>): void;
  /**
   * The pointer reached the right edge in fullscreen (`true`) or left the popped-out sidebar (`false`): the attached sidebar pops out or collapses (reference §6.3). No effect outside fullscreen, when hidden or floating.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Pop the sidebar out in fullscreen
   * The pointer reaches the right edge in fullscreen and the attached
   * sidebar pops out over the video. Outside fullscreen, or with the
   * sidebar hidden or floating, nothing happens.
   * ```ts
   * host.setMainWindow({ fullscreen: true });
   * host.popSidebar(true);
   * await host.settle();
   * ```
   */
  popSidebar(popped: boolean): void;
  /**
   * Simulate another plugin (or the user) opening a source: a new `sourceId`, then the given phase. Calls the plugin made against the old state now fail with `stale`.
   * @param source - The path or URL.
   * @param phase - The phase to end in (default `"ready"`).
   * @capability None.
   * @example Let the user open another file meanwhile
   * A state the plugin captured before stops being current once another
   * file opens. `openElsewhere` gives the source a new `sourceId`, so
   * `isCurrent` turns false. Promise-returning calls made with
   * `ifCurrent: before` then reject with `stale`; calls that return nothing
   * drop the write silently instead (`TimelineLayer.set` with `ifCurrent`).
   * ```ts
   * const before = plugin.player.state;
   * host.openElsewhere("/media/other.mp4");
   * await host.settle();
   * assert.equal(plugin.player.isCurrent(before), false);
   * ```
   */
  openElsewhere(source: string, phase?: SourceState["phase"]): void;
  /**
   * Simulate a generated stream failing in the player (its audio device lost, its frame connection broken), like the player: the source fails with `message` (`phase: "error"`) and the producer is retired at once. The stream's `onStop` listeners get a `stream` error with `message`.
   * @param producerId - The producer, from TestHost.producers.
   * @param message - The player's failure text.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Break the plugin's generated stream
   * The plugin's stream stops with an error, as when the player loses its
   * audio device. `failStream` puts the source into `error` with the
   * message and retires the producer at once; the stream's `onStop`
   * listeners get a `stream` error carrying the message.
   * ```ts
   * const [producer] = host.producers.values();
   * host.failStream(producer!.id, "producer transport closed");
   * ```
   */
  failStream(producerId: number, message: string): void;
  /**
   * Press a binding like the host's table would: panel-focus bindings first when `panel` is true, then global ones; within a scope the earliest registration first (the player's own commands before the plugin's), as the conflict rule orders them. A disabled command lets the key pass to the next command bound to it (SDK 1.5.12, as player 0.4.3): the one it shadowed, then the global scope. The first enabled one runs; `press` resolves after it ran (`"ran"`). When only disabled commands hold the key, the first of them decides, as in the player: with a `reason` it shows the reason on the OSD and eats the key (`"reason"`, see `host.osd`); without one the key goes on to the focused control (`"passed"`, nothing runs). Unlike the player, which only logs a key that reaches a busy command, `press` then rejects, so a test notices. Rejects when nothing is bound. Bindings use the reference syntax (`"Space"`, `"Ctrl+O"`, `"Mouse:WheelUp"`), and user overrides in `bindings.overlay` apply.
   * @returns What the key did: `"ran"`, `"reason"` or `"passed"`.
   * @capability None.
   * @throws command (rejects) A `HostError`: the command that would run is busy (the player only logs this).
   * @throws Error (rejects) Nothing is bound to the key.
   * @example Press a global key and a panel key
   * Ctrl+B runs whatever is bound globally; Delete is pressed while the
   * plugin's panel has focus, so panel bindings are tried first. `press`
   * follows the player's binding table and resolves with what happened:
   * `"ran"`, `"reason"` (a disabled command showed why) or `"passed"`.
   * ```ts
   * await host.press("Ctrl+B"); // a global binding
   * await host.press("Delete", { panel: true }); // while the panel has focus
   * ```
   */
  press(binding: string, options?: {
    panel?: boolean;
  }): Promise<"ran" | "reason" | "passed">;
  /**
   * Bindings declared by more than one command, each as `[binding, winner, ...ignored]` (command ids; core actions as `host/<id>`). Empty when there are none.
   * @example Check that no default keys collide
   * The test fails when two commands, the player's or the plugin's, declare
   * the same binding. Each entry is `[binding, winner, ...ignored]`, so an
   * empty list means every key does what its command says.
   * ```ts
   * assert.deepEqual(host.conflicts, []);
   * ```
   */
  get conflicts(): string[][];
  /** The binding overlay `plugin.bindings.set` writes (`"<plugin>/<command>"` to inputs; preset it to simulate saved overrides). `press` honours it. */
  readonly bindings: {
    /** `"<plugin>/<command>"` → the user's inputs for it. */
    overlay: Map<string, string[]>;
  };
  /**
   * What `packages.list` reports; `setEnabled`, `uninstall` and `install` update it. `builtin`, `source` and `dataDirectory` are optional here (default `false`, `null`, `null`).
   */
  packages: {
    /** The plugin's manifest id. */
    id: string;
    /** Its version, `null` when unknown. */
    version: string | null;
    /** Where it was loaded from. */
    origin: "installed" | "development";
    /** Its run state. */
    state: "starting" | "running" | "disabled" | "failed" | "stopped";
    /** Why it failed (`state: "failed"`). */
    error: string | null;
    /** Its declared capabilities. */
    capabilities: string[];
    /** The package directory. */
    directory: string;
    /** Shipped with the player: `uninstall` and `install` are `unsupported`. */
    builtin?: boolean;
    /** Where it was installed from. */
    source?: PackageSource | null;
    /** Its data directory. */
    dataDirectory?: string | null;
  }[];
  /** Every `packages.setEnabled` / `uninstall` / `install`, newest last. */
  readonly packageCalls: {
    /** Which call. */
    method: "setEnabled" | "reload" | "uninstall" | "install";
    /** The target plugin id. */
    id: string;
    /** `setEnabled`'s value. */
    enabled?: boolean;
    /** `uninstall`'s `removeData` option. */
    removeData?: boolean;
    /** `install`'s source (`{ kind: "file" }` when not given). */
    source?: PackageSource;
    /** `install`'s `replace` option. */
    replace?: boolean;
  }[];
  /**
   * Packages `validate` and `validateArchive` accept: path (directory or `.vxp` file) → its manifest. Other paths fail with `missing`. `install` adds or upgrades the entry in TestHost.packages following the player's source rules: the same source upgrades, another source needs `replace` (`conflict` otherwise), a built-in id is `unsupported`.
   * @example Offer a package file the plugin can install
   * The plugin can validate and install `/downloads/someone.demo-1.0.0.vxp`
   * as if the file existed. The host accepts only paths listed here (others
   * fail with `missing`) and returns this manifest from `validate`; an
   * install then follows the player's source rules.
   * ```ts
   * host.candidates.set("/downloads/someone.demo-1.0.0.vxp", {
   *   id: "someone.demo", version: "1.0.0", apiVersion: "vestra/1",
   *   entry: "main.js", capabilities: [],
   * });
   * ```
   */
  readonly candidates: Map<string, PackageManifest>;
  /**
   * Remote images (`plugin.ui.markdown`, `plugin.ui.remoteImage`): address → a local PNG or JPEG file served for it, or `null` for a failing download. Nothing is fetched from the network in tests; unknown addresses fail.
   */
  readonly remoteImages: Map<string, string | null>;
  /**
   * The Markdown document a value holds (its wire form read back), or `null` when the value is not one. `images` maps each remote address to the downloaded file. Pass a whole property value or a field of one: a document nested in rows is read the same way.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Read back a Markdown message in a chat window
   * The test checks the Markdown source of the first chat message. Rows
   * hold the document in its wire form, as `plugin.ui.markdown` produced
   * it; `markdown` reads it back, nested in a row or not.
   * ```ts
   * const rows = host.window("chat").props["messages"] as { body: Json }[];
   * assert.equal(host.markdown(rows[0]!.body)?.text, "**Hello**");
   * ```
   */
  markdown(value: Json | undefined): MarkdownWire | null;
  /** What `player.audioDevices()` lists. `setAudioDevice` updates `host.source.audioOutput`. */
  audioDevices: {
    /** The device id, e.g. `coreaudio/<UID>`. */
    id: string;
    /** The system's name for it. */
    name: string;
  }[];
  /**
   * Replace the plugin list and push `packages.changed` (another plugin started, stopped, was installed or removed).
   * @capability None.
   * @example Simulate another plugin starting
   * The plugin's store window hears that a plugin is running now. The list
   * replaces `packages` and is pushed as `packages.changed`, which the
   * plugin's `packages.onChange` listeners receive.
   * ```ts
   * host.setPackages([...host.packages]); // edit a copy, then push it
   * await host.settle();
   * ```
   */
  setPackages(list: TestHost["packages"]): void;
  /**
   * Simulate another plugin calling `player.next()` / `previous()`: the host asks this plugin's sequence provider. Rejects with `unavailable` when there is no provider or its flag is false.
   * @capability None.
   * @throws unavailable (rejects) A `HostError`: there is no sequence provider, or its flag is false.
   * @example Ask the plugin's provider for the next item
   * Another plugin calls `player.next()`; the host asks the plugin under
   * test, which is the sequence provider, and the test checks what it
   * opened.
   * ```ts
   * await host.step("next");
   * await host.settle();
   * assert.equal(host.source.source, "/media/b.mp4");
   * ```
   */
  step(direction: "next" | "previous"): Promise<unknown>;
  /**
   * The plugin's command with this local id. Throws when it is not registered (never added, or disposed).
   * @capability None.
   * @example Read a command's state after a change
   * The test checks that Export becomes enabled once a file is ready. The
   * record is updated as the plugin sends new state; read it after
   * `settle()`.
   * ```ts
   * host.setSource({ phase: "ready", duration: 60 });
   * await host.settle();
   * assert.equal(host.command("export").state.enabled, true); // throws if not registered
   * ```
   */
  command(id: string): FakeCommand;
  /**
   * The plugin's bottom-bar buttons (`CommandOptions.button`) as the player shows them: at most one, the first declared (`BAR_BUTTON_LIMITS`; a later one stays a menu item only). Empty once the command is disposed. Whether the bar places them is the bar's business: the list is what the player hands to `BarButtons`.
   * @example Click the plugin's bottom-bar button in a test
   * The test finds the plugin's Store button, clicks it and checks that the
   * Store window opened. `barButtons` lists the buttons of the plugin's
   * commands declared with `button`, as the bar shows them; `click()` runs
   * the command like its menu item and waits until the host is idle, and
   * rejects while the command is disabled or busy.
   * ```ts
   * const [button] = host.barButtons; // one button per plugin
   * assert.equal(button?.icon, "store");
   * await button?.click();
   * assert.equal(host.window("store").visible, true);
   * ```
   */
  get barButtons(): readonly FakeBarButton[];
  /**
   * The plugin's tool window with this id (by default the file name without extension: `ui/picture.slint` → `picture`). Throws when it was never opened with `show()`.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Press a window's Reset button from a test
   * The Picture window's Reset callback runs and the brightness returns to
   * 0. The window is found by its id (the `.slint` file name by default);
   * `emit` fires the callback the plugin bound, and `settle()` waits for
   * the property the handler wrote.
   * ```ts
   * host.window("picture").emit("reset");
   * await host.settle();
   * assert.equal(host.window("picture").props["brightness"], 0);
   * ```
   */
  window(id: string): FakeWindow;
  /**
   * The plugin's mounted panel (bottom bar, sidebar or backdrop). Throws when none is mounted. Its `props` use Slint (kebab-case) names; `emit` fires a callback on the panel's global.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Select a row in the plugin's sidebar panel
   * The test checks the panel sits in the sidebar and selects its third
   * row. `emit` fires a callback on the panel's global as a click would;
   * the plugin's handler runs, and `settle()` waits for what it sent.
   * ```ts
   * const panel = host.mounted();
   * assert.equal(panel.slot, "sidebar");
   * panel.emit("select", 2);
   * await host.settle();
   * ```
   */
  mounted(): Omit<FakeWindow, "callbacks" | "userClose"> & {
    /** `"bottom"`, `"sidebar"` or `"backdrop"`. */
    slot: string;
    /** The exported component the SDK found in the file. */
    component: string;
    /** The last `panel.setInteraction(...)` locks, `null` before any. */
    locks: Json;
  };
  /**
   * The parameters of every request of one wire method, oldest first.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Check the request behind an OSD message
   * The test checks the last OSD request the plugin sent, before
   * translation. `sent` lists the parameters of every request of one wire
   * method, oldest first; `host.osd` holds the texts as shown instead.
   * ```ts
   * assert.deepEqual(host.sent("osd.show").at(-1), { text: "Saved" });
   * ```
   */
  sent(method: string): Record<string, Json>[];
  /**
   * Wait until no request is in flight (and the SDK's follow-up passes ran),
   * and at least `ms` milliseconds have passed so that timers due by then
   * fired. Call it after every action that makes the plugin talk to the host,
   * before asserting.
   *
   * It only waits for host calls. Work the plugin does on its own (reading
   * or parsing a file, a child process, a network request) is not waited
   * for: on a loaded machine it can finish after `settle()` returns. Poll
   * the result you assert on instead (second example).
   * @param ms - Extra time to wait, for debounces and timers (default 0).
   * @capability None.
   * @throws Never.
   * @example Wait past a debounced save
   * The plugin's store writes its file 300 ms after the last `save`, so
   * the test waits 400 ms before it checks what the plugin did next.
   * `settle(ms)` returns when no request is in flight and at least `ms`
   * have passed, so the store's timer has fired. The file write itself is
   * the plugin's own work, which `settle` does not wait for: a test that
   * reads the file calls `await store.flush()` instead.
   * ```ts
   * const store = plugin.storage.json("prefs", { defaults: { step: 5 } });
   * store.save({ step: 10 });
   * await host.settle(400); // past storage.json's 300 ms debounce
   * ```
   * @example Poll for work the plugin does on its own
   * The plugin reads and parses a file before it shows a status; `settle`
   * does not wait for that (it only waits for host requests), so the test
   * polls the property it asserts on, 20 ms at a time, for up to 2 seconds.
   * ```ts
   * const window = host.window("import");
   * window.emit("load-file"); // the plugin reads and parses the file itself
   * for (let i = 0; i < 100 && window.props["status-text"] !== expected; i++)
   *   await host.settle(20);
   * assert.equal(window.props["status-text"], expected);
   * ```
   */
  settle(ms?: number): Promise<void>;
  /**
   * Close the fake stream servers and delete the host's temporary directories. `stop()` from startPlugin calls it.
   * @capability None.
   * @example Clean up a host that was never started
   * A test that made a host but failed before `startPlugin` removes the
   * host's temporary directories itself. `stop()` from `startPlugin` calls
   * `close` for you otherwise.
   * ```ts
   * const host = new TestHost();
   * try {
   *   // … preset the host; the test fails here …
   * } finally {
   *   host.close(); // deletes the host's temporary data
   * }
   * ```
   */
  close(): void;
}
```

Example: Preset the player, then react to another plugin's file

The test starts the plugin in a player with the dark theme, opens a file
the way another plugin would, and checks the plugin's panel title. A host
created first can be preset with data the plugin reads during
activation; `startPlugin` then uses it. `openElsewhere` changes the
source and broadcasts it, the plugin's listener updates its panel, and
`settle()` waits for those requests before the assertion.
```ts
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import test from "node:test";
import { startPlugin, TestHost } from "@vestra-player/sdk/testing";
import activate from "../main.ts";

test("shows the playing file in the panel", async () => {
  const host = new TestHost();
  host.appearance = "vestra"; // read during activation
  const { stop } = await startPlugin(activate, {
    directory: new URL("..", import.meta.url),
    host,
  });
  host.openElsewhere("/media/clip.mp4"); // another plugin opened a file
  await host.settle();
  assert.equal(host.mounted().props["title"], "clip.mp4");
  await stop();
});
```

### startPlugin

Activate a plugin against a test host, the way the player's runner does:
build the `plugin` object, call `activate(plugin)`, wait for every
registration started during activation (commands, panels, resolvers, ...),
then wait until the host is idle.

The manifest id and capabilities come from `directory/manifest.json`
unless `capabilities` is given; then `id` (default `"test.plugin"`) and
`capabilities` are used and no manifest is read. Calls that need an
undeclared capability fail with `capability`, as in the player.

Rejects when `manifest.json` cannot be read or parsed, when `activate`
throws, or when a registration made during activation fails (for example
`limit`, `conflict`, `invalid`), which is when the player would fail the
activation.

The way into a plugin's tests: one call starts the plugin the way the
player's runner does and returns the host to drive, the `plugin` object
to call directly, and `stop` to end it like the player.

- @param activate - The plugin's default-exported `activate` function.
- @param options - Where the plugin lives and how to start it.
- @returns `host`: the TestHost; `plugin`: the object passed to `activate` (call the plugin API on it directly); `stop()`: dispose the plugin like the player stopping it (scopes released, stores flushed), wait until the host is idle and remove the host's temporary files.
- @capability None.

```ts
function startPlugin(activate: (plugin: Plugin) => unknown, options?: {
  /**
   * The plugin's package directory, as a path or a `file:` URL (e.g. `new URL("..", import.meta.url)` from `tests/`). Relative `.slint` files resolve against it. Default: the current working directory.
   */
  directory?: string | URL;
  /** The manifest id when `capabilities` is given. Default `"test.plugin"`. */
  id?: string;
  /** Use these capabilities instead of reading `manifest.json`. */
  capabilities?: string[];
  /** A host to use (to preset data before activation). Default: a new one. */
  host?: TestHost;
  /** Use an existing directory as `plugin.dataDirectory` (to test a restart). */
  dataDirectory?: string;
  /**
   * Start with these `plugin.storage.session` values (to test a restart within one player session): pass the previous run's `host.sessionStorage`. They are copied into the new host's TestHost.sessionStorage.
   */
  sessionStorage?: ReadonlyMap<string, Json>;
  /**
   * The interface language to play (TestHost.locale): the plugin's `locales/<locale>.po` (or `.json`) in `directory` is loaded and its menus, messages and titles show translated. Default: the host's.
   */
  locale?: Locale;
}): Promise<{
  /** The test host the plugin talks to. */
  host: TestHost;
  /** The `plugin` object passed to `activate`. */
  plugin: Plugin;
  /** Stop the plugin, wait for the host, and remove temporary files. */
  stop(): Promise<void>;
}>;
```

Example: Test that a setting survives a restart

The test turns on the 10-step option, stops the plugin, starts it again
on the same data directory and checks the option is still on. Both runs
get a directory the test made (`dataDirectory`): `stop()` disposes the
plugin like the player, which writes its pending stores there, and only
removes the host's own temporary directory, so the second run reads what
the first one saved.
```ts
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { mkdtempSync, rmSync } from "node:fs";
import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
import { join } from "node:path";
import test from "node:test";
import { startPlugin } from "@vestra-player/sdk/testing";
import activate from "../main.ts";

test("remembers the step across restarts", async () => {
  const directory = new URL("..", import.meta.url);
  const data = mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), "data-"));
  try {
    const first = await startPlugin(activate, { directory, dataDirectory: data });
    try {
      await first.host.command("step-10").run();
    } finally {
      await first.stop(); // flushes the plugin's stores into `data`
    }

    // A restart: a new host and a new plugin instance on the same data.
    const second = await startPlugin(activate, { directory, dataDirectory: data });
    try {
      assert.equal(second.host.command("step-10").state.checked, true);
    } finally {
      await second.stop();
    }
  } finally {
    rmSync(data, { recursive: true, force: true });
  }
});
```

### CapabilityInfo

What one manifest capability is for: the members it opens, the
capabilities they also need, and how the plugin store describes it. An
entry of CAPABILITY_INFO.

```ts
interface CapabilityInfo {
  /**
   * The members this capability opens, as `Interface.member` (for example `Commands.add` is `plugin.commands.add`). A call to one of them without the capability fails with code `capability`; `Plugin.video.filter` is `plugin.video.filter`. A member can be listed under more than one capability when it needs all of them (`Panel.onChange` needs `ui.mount` and `events`).
   */
  readonly apis: readonly string[];
  /**
   * Capabilities every member in CapabilityInfo.apis also needs: declare them as well. What only one member or one option needs (`Plugin.video.filter` also needs `events`) is documented at that member.
   */
  readonly requires: readonly string[];
  /**
   * How the plugin store and the player's install confirmation describe the capability to the user, in English (the player translates it). Two capabilities can share one description (`media.read` and `media.control`); the store then shows it once.
   */
  readonly label: string;
  /**
   * `true` when the store highlights the capability as one to think about before installing (it reaches outside the plugin's own features: the clipboard, every shortcut, the keychain, other plugins).
   */
  readonly risky: boolean;
}
```

### CAPABILITY_INFO

Every manifest capability the player knows (`vestra/1`), in the player's
order, with the members it opens, the capabilities they also need and the
store's wording. Built from the player's own capability table (its
`src/host/capabilities.json`, copied into the SDK) and the requests each
member sends, the same rule `vestra-plugin check` and the SDK's
TypeScript plugin apply; the player's tests check that the copy is
current.

A member not listed under any capability needs none (`plugin.tools`,
`plugin.storage`, `plugin.system`, `plugin.app`, `plugin.ui`,
`plugin.i18n`, reading `plugin.window.state`, `plugin.appearance.theme`,
`plugin.packages.list` and `plugin.rendering.state`).

```ts
const CAPABILITY_INFO: Readonly<Record<string, CapabilityInfo>>;
```

Example: Check in a test that the manifest declares every required capability

The test fails, naming the missing capability, when the manifest declares
a capability without one its members also need. It reads the plugin's own
`manifest.json` and looks each declared name up in `CAPABILITY_INFO`,
whose `requires` lists the capabilities that must be declared with it;
at run time the player would refuse such a call with code `capability`.
```ts
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { CAPABILITY_INFO } from "@vestra-player/sdk/testing";

const manifest: { capabilities: string[] } = JSON.parse(
  await readFile(new URL("../manifest.json", import.meta.url), "utf8"),
);
for (const capability of manifest.capabilities)
  // An unknown name has no entry: `vestra-plugin check` reports it.
  for (const needed of CAPABILITY_INFO[capability]?.requires ?? [])
    assert.ok(manifest.capabilities.includes(needed), needed);
```

### MESSAGE_LIMIT

The longest message a plugin may send the player, in UTF-8 bytes of one
protocol line with its newline (1 MiB). The player stops a plugin that
writes a longer one, so the plugin's side refuses such a request before
sending it: it rejects with code `limit`. Property values meet
UI_VALUE_LIMITS before this.

```ts
const MESSAGE_LIMIT: number;
```

### COMMAND_LIMITS

The player's command registry caps, the same values as the player's own
table (the player's tests check that they agree). They are runaway guards,
not product limits: a command added past them is refused by the player
with code `limit` (its `ready` rejects; during activation, activation
fails; later the failure goes to `Scope.onError`), commands
already registered are unaffected, and disposing a command frees its slot
at once. TestHost enforces the same caps.

For menus built from media content (tracks, chapters, presets), set your
own sensible display cap well below `perPlugin`.

```ts
const COMMAND_LIMITS: {
  /** Commands one plugin instance may have at the same time (160). */
  readonly perPlugin: 160;
  /** Commands of every plugin plus the player's own, together (1024). */
  readonly total: 1024;
};
```

Example: Cap a chapter menu well below the command limit

The Chapters submenu lists at most 50 chapters, however many the file
has. Every menu item is a command, and the player counts them per plugin.
`add` itself returns at once and never throws `limit`: past `perPlugin`
the player refuses the registration, which fails the activation or, later,
reaches `Scope.onError`. A try/catch around `add` cannot catch that, so a
menu built from media content keeps its own cap and leaves room for the
plugin's fixed commands.
```ts
import { COMMAND_LIMITS } from "@vestra-player/sdk/testing";

// 20 slots stay free for the plugin's own commands.
const shown = chapters.slice(0, Math.min(50, COMMAND_LIMITS.perPlugin - 20));
```

### MENU_IDS

The player's built-in top-level menus, by id. Write `@<id>` as the first
segment of a command path (`["@video", "Blur"]`, see `CommandOptions.path`) to put a
command into that menu whatever language the player's menus are in. The
player stores the menu's title (视频 today); later segments are titles.
Needs player 0.3.0 (`"minPlayerVersion": "0.3.0"`); older players show
`@video` as a menu of its own. The player's tests check that this list
agrees with the player's.

```ts
const MENU_IDS: readonly ["open", "playback", "subtitles", "video", "audio", "screen", "settings"];
```

Example: Put a command into the built-in Video menu

"Blur" appears in the player's Video menu in every interface language.
The player replaces a leading `@video` with that menu's key ("Video")
before it merges paths, so the item joins the built-in menu; an id that
is not in `MENU_IDS` makes `add` fail with `invalid`, which a test can
rule out ahead of time.
```ts
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { MENU_IDS } from "@vestra-player/sdk/testing";

plugin.commands.add({ id: "blur", path: ["@video", "Blur"], run() {} });
assert.ok(MENU_IDS.includes("video")); // a menu id, not a title
```

### BAR_BUTTON_ICONS

The icons a bottom-bar button may name (`CommandOptions.button.icon`):
every icon of the player's V-Line set, `@vestra/icons.slint` (draw one
in your own Slint with `Icon { name: "store"; }`). The player's tests check
that this list is its icon set.

```ts
const BAR_BUTTON_ICONS: readonly ["play", "pause", "stop", "back", "forward", "open", "volume", "mute", "playlist", "detach", "attach", "close", "failed", "move-top", "move-up", "move-down", "move-bottom", "search", "chapter", "bookmark", "check-task", "check-box", "menu-check", "submenu", "scroll-up", "scroll-down", "caret-down", "sort-asc", "sort-desc", "tag-remove", "preview-play", "add", "remove", "sort", "fullscreen", "exit-fullscreen", "store", "ai"];
```

Example: Check in a test that the button's icon exists

The test fails before release if the plugin's bar button names an icon
the player does not have. `commands.add` would refuse an unknown name
with `invalid`; the player's tests keep `BAR_BUTTON_ICONS` equal to its
icon set, so checking against it is the same check without a player.
```ts
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { BAR_BUTTON_ICONS } from "@vestra-player/sdk/testing";

assert.ok(BAR_BUTTON_ICONS.includes("store")); // the icon main.ts uses
```

### BAR_BUTTON_LIMITS

The player's limits on bottom-bar buttons (`CommandOptions.button`), the
same values as the player's (its tests check that they agree). A button
past `perPlugin` or `total` is left out: its command still registers and
its menu entry stays, and the player logs the button it left out
(`limit`). Which ones stay: each plugin's first declared button, then the
`total` highest by order, plugin id and declaration order: as in a narrow
strip, the lowest order goes first (equal orders: the smaller plugin id,
then the earlier declaration, goes first).

```ts
const BAR_BUTTON_LIMITS: {
  /** Buttons one plugin shows (1). */
  readonly perPlugin: 1;
  /** Buttons the player shows, every plugin together, besides its own sidebar toggle (8). */
  readonly total: 8;
  /** The highest `order` (999; the lowest is 0). */
  readonly maxOrder: 999;
};
```

### BuiltinSubmenu

A submenu that one of the player's built-in plugins declares: an entry of
BUILTIN_SUBMENUS.

```ts
interface BuiltinSubmenu {
  /**
   * The submenu's key path: the English texts paths merge by, the built-in menu first by its key (`"Playback"` for `@playback`). Write these segments, followed by your command's title, to put a command into this submenu.
   */
  readonly path: readonly string[];
  /** The built-in plugins that declare it (`vestra.history`). */
  readonly plugins: readonly string[];
}
```

### BUILTIN_SUBMENUS

The submenus the player's built-in plugins declare, by key path, in menu
order (built-in menus as in MENU_IDS, then top-level submenus).
Menu paths merge by their English key, so a command whose path starts
with the same keys appears in the same submenu, whatever the interface
language; the submenu's title is the declaring plugin's translation. The
player's own submenus (`Playback ▸ Speed`, `Playback ▸ Seek`) are not
listed. The player's tests check that this list agrees with what its
built-in plugins declare.

```ts
const BUILTIN_SUBMENUS: readonly BuiltinSubmenu[];
```

Example: Add an item to the built-in Snapshot submenu

"Copy Snapshot" appears in Video ▸ Snapshot next to the built-in capture
plugin's items. Paths merge by their English keys, so a command whose
path continues with the submenu's keys (`["Video", "Snapshot"]`, the menu
written as `@video`) lands in the same submenu whatever the interface
language.
```ts
import { BUILTIN_SUBMENUS } from "@vestra-player/sdk/testing";

const snapshot = BUILTIN_SUBMENUS.find((menu) => menu.path.at(-1) === "Snapshot")!;
plugin.commands.add({
  id: "snapshot-to-clipboard",
  // ["@video", "Snapshot", "Copy Snapshot"]; @video stands for "Video".
  path: ["@video", ...snapshot.path.slice(1), "Copy Snapshot"],
  run: copySnapshot,
});
```

### BuiltinCommand

A command the player or one of its built-in plugins registers: an entry
of BUILTIN_COMMANDS.

```ts
interface BuiltinCommand {
  /** `"host"` for the player's own commands, else the built-in plugin's id. */
  readonly owner: string;
  /** The command's id within its owner (`"play-pause"`, `"capture.save"`). */
  readonly id: string;
  /**
   * The menu path by key (the English texts paths merge by), the leaf included; a built-in menu by its key (`"Video"`, not `"@video"`). Empty for a command that is not in the main menu (a panel shortcut).
   */
  readonly path: readonly string[];
  /** The English title (the last segment of `path` when there is one). */
  readonly title: string;
  /** The default bindings, canonical, in the order the command declares them. */
  readonly bindings: readonly string[];
  /** `"panel"`: the bindings apply only while the owner's panel has focus. */
  readonly focus: "panel" | null;
}
```

### BUILTIN_COMMANDS

The commands the player and its built-in plugins register when the
player starts with nothing open, in menu order (commands outside the main
menu last): their key paths, default bindings and owners. Use it to pick
a menu place and default keys that do not collide with the player's (the
user's own changes come on top; see Bindings). Menu items built
from content (tracks, recent files, output devices) are not listed; their
placeholders (`No Audio Tracks`) are. The player's tests check that this
list agrees with what the player and its built-in plugins register.

```ts
const BUILTIN_COMMANDS: readonly BuiltinCommand[];
```

Example: Check in a test that a default key is still free

The test fails if the player or a built-in plugin already binds Ctrl+K
globally, before users ever see a conflict. It collects the default
bindings of every built-in command that is not limited to its panel's
focus (`focus: null`) and looks for the key the plugin wants; bindings
are canonical, so compare them as the player writes them.
```ts
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { BUILTIN_COMMANDS } from "@vestra-player/sdk/testing";

const taken = BUILTIN_COMMANDS.filter((command) => command.focus === null)
  .flatMap((command) => command.bindings);
assert.ok(!taken.includes("Ctrl+K"));
```

### LOCALES

The player's interface languages: English (the source language) first,
then the translations, as the player's own table (its tests check that
they agree).

```ts
const LOCALES: readonly ["en", "zh-Hans", "ja", "ko", "de", "fr", "es"];
```

### LIST_SEPARATORS

The separator of each list style per interface language, as the player's
table (`i18n::text::SEPARATORS`; its tests check that they agree).

```ts
const LIST_SEPARATORS: Readonly<Record<Locale, Readonly<Record<ListStyle, string>>>>;
```

### TEXT_LIMITS

The player's limits on one text value (a
Text or
TextList with everything nested in it), as the player's
`i18n::text` (its tests check that they agree).

```ts
const TEXT_LIMITS: {
  /** Nesting depth of texts and lists; the value itself is depth 0 (8). */
  readonly depth: 8;
  /** Texts, lists and arguments in all, the value itself included (1024). */
  readonly nodes: 1024;
  /** Arguments of one text (16). */
  readonly args: 16;
  /** Items of one list (256). */
  readonly items: 256;
  /** UTF-8 bytes of a source text or a string argument (4096). */
  readonly stringBytes: 4096;
};
```

### THEME_PALETTES

The colours of the player's palettes, by `Theme` colour token (without the
`Theme.` prefix): `vestra`, the dark default, and `vestra-light` (player
0.4.0). The player sets one of them on every view; a plugin reads the
colours through `Theme` in its Slint files and never needs these values.
They are here for the documentation (Reference: theme) and for tests that
check a design against both palettes.

Current values: a later player may adjust them, a token keeps its
meaning. The `vestra` values are also the defaults of the SDK's copy of
the palette (`slint/palette.slint`); the player's tests check both
palettes against its own.

```ts
const THEME_PALETTES: Readonly<Record<"vestra" | "vestra-light", Readonly<Record<string, string>>>>;
```

Example: Check in a test that a colour stays readable in both themes

The test fails if the plugin's own highlight colour gets too close to
the panel background of either palette. Plugins draw with `Theme` tokens
in Slint and the player switches palettes; a colour the plugin picks
itself does not switch, so a test compares it with each palette's values
(hex strings, `#rrggbb`).
```ts
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { THEME_PALETTES } from "@vestra-player/sdk/testing";

const highlight = "#e07000"; // the plugin's own orange
const luminance = (hex: string) => {
  const [r, g, b] = [1, 3, 5].map((i) => parseInt(hex.slice(i, i + 2), 16) / 255);
  return 0.2126 * r! + 0.7152 * g! + 0.0722 * b!; // rough, without gamma
};
for (const [name, palette] of Object.entries(THEME_PALETTES)) {
  const gap = Math.abs(luminance(highlight) - luminance(palette["bg-panel"]!));
  assert.ok(gap > 0.3, `${name}: highlight too close to bg-panel`);
}
```

### BINDING_INPUTS

The names a binding (`CommandOptions.bindings`, `Bindings.set`) is made
of, as the player's binding parser accepts them. A binding is
`{ modifier "+" } input`: modifiers in the order of `modifiers`, each at
most once, then one input. An input is a name of `letters`, `digits`,
`functionKeys`, `named` or `mouse`, or one other printable character that
is not a letter, digit, space or `+` (`">"`, `"["`, `"/"`), written as
typed, never with `Shift` (`">"`, not `"Shift+."`; `"!"`, not
`"Shift+1"`). Anything else fails with code `invalid`. The player's tests
check that these agree with the player.

```ts
const BINDING_INPUTS: Readonly<{
  /** Modifiers, in the order a binding writes them. `Cmd` is ⌘ on macOS and the Windows logo key on Windows; on macOS `Ctrl` also matches ⌘. */
  readonly modifiers: readonly ["Ctrl", "Alt", "Shift", "Cmd"];
  /** Letter keys, by key name whatever the case: `A` to `Z`. */
  readonly letters: readonly string[];
  /** Digit keys of the main keyboard: `0` to `9`. */
  readonly digits: readonly string[];
  /** Function keys: `F1` to `F24`. */
  readonly functionKeys: string[];
  /**
   * Other named keys, matched by the physical key. `Plus` is the `+` key however it is typed; the `Numpad…` names are the numeric keypad only, never the main keyboard.
   */
  readonly named: readonly ["Space", "Enter", "Tab", "Escape", "Backspace", "Delete", "Insert", "Home", "End", "PageUp", "PageDown", "ArrowLeft", "ArrowRight", "ArrowUp", "ArrowDown", "Plus", ...string[], "NumpadPlus", "NumpadMinus", "NumpadMultiply", "NumpadDivide", "NumpadEnter", "NumpadDecimal"];
  /** Mouse inputs on the video area. `:LeftHalf` and `:RightHalf` tell the halves of the video apart for a double click. */
  readonly mouse: readonly ["Mouse:LeftClick", "Mouse:LeftDoubleClick", "Mouse:LeftDoubleClick:LeftHalf", "Mouse:LeftDoubleClick:RightHalf", "Mouse:MiddleClick", "Mouse:X1", "Mouse:X2", "Mouse:WheelUp", "Mouse:WheelDown", "Mouse:WheelLeft", "Mouse:WheelRight"];
}>;
```

Example: Check in a test that the plugin's default keys are well formed
